sources.title: How Theo went from Twitch engineer to YC founder, creator, and T3 Chat CEO
sources.originalTitle: The painful truth about startups (my story)
sources.summary: Theo walks through his chaotic path: Twitch, a music startup, T3 Tools/Ping, YC, accidental YouTube success, laying off his team after overhiring, and finally T3 Chat. The lesson is that he never predicted the winners, only recognized wrong paths, built things he wanted, and stayed close to users.

principles.text: Make something people want by building something you deeply want yourself, then compromise to serve others' needs.
principles.quote: it's much easier to make something people want. If you are people, if you're making something that you want deeply enough, that you care about that solves a problem you have.

principles.text: Don't overhire or cosplay as a big company; headcount and branding don't matter if the product doesn't earn.
principles.quote: I was cosplaying as a big company when I wasn't. I had hired too many people.

principles.text: Selling tools to creators is a non-starter; developer tools are far easier to get adopted and monetize.
principles.quote: If you're building a tool that's exclusive customer base is creators and influencers, you are going to struggle immensely to even make money, much less be a scalable business.

principles.text: Winning a market of users who don't pay or stick around yields little revenue; check who actually spends.
principles.quote: Winning half the streamers makes you no money because streamers don't spend a lot of money and they don't stick around for a long time.

principles.text: Aim to be default alive: stack small profitable products until revenue covers costs and you can't die from running out of money.
principles.quote: We were as YC phrases it default alive. if we didn't grow anymore, we wouldn't go out of business.

principles.text: You can't predict what wins; keep acknowledging wrong paths and trying new ones while caring about users and quality.
principles.quote: at no point did I correctly predict what was next for us. I could only ever see what wasn't.

sources.title: Why managed services beat raw AWS on real cost: free tiers, engineer time, and scale-to-zero
sources.originalTitle: The REAL Cost Of AWS (And How To Avoid It)
sources.summary: Theo argues that "AWS is cheaper" claims miss three things: generous free tiers carry small projects a long way, engineer time is the biggest hidden cost, and managed services let you build in ways that cost less to run. His takeaway is that most teams self-hosting need a very good reason, because they are usually spending more.

principles.text: Generous free tiers on modern managed services carry most small projects far; check them before assuming you need raw cloud.
principles.quote: the free tier carries you really far

principles.text: Engineer time is the real cost of DIY infrastructure; setup and maintenance hours dwarf small monthly savings.
principles.quote: we're talking hundreds upon hundreds of hours and whether or not I like to admit it that's expensive

principles.text: Spend engineering time on product differentiation, not on shaving the infrastructure bill.
principles.quote: your engineer should be spending time making your product better for your users so you can beat your competition not making your AWS cheaper

principles.text: Don't rewrite onto self-hosted infrastructure to cut cost until a service is stable and high-traffic; most teams are far from that point.
principles.quote: most of us are very far from that point even y'all working at big companies because most code is changing and the cost of change is high

principles.text: Usage-based, scale-to-zero billing aligns cost with traffic; running servers means paying for idle compute.
principles.quote: if you're running servers you're paying for a compute that isn't being used period

principles.text: Caching responses is far cheaper than computing every request; invalidate only on real changes.
principles.quote: it's so much cheaper to Cache a response than to run a server that processes every single request like comically

sources.title: Build the tool you need: why Theo made free SVG-to-PNG and square-image tools
sources.originalTitle: This tool annoyed me (so I built a free version)
sources.summary: Theo built two free, open-source browser tools (SVG to PNG, square image generator) because existing options were slow, paywalled, or lacked basic features. His takeaway: solving your own annoying problem is the most reliable way to find products people want, as with UploadThing, Pick Thing, and his channel itself.

principles.text: Build the thing you personally need; own-use-case products tend to blow up.
principles.quote: some of the most successful things I have built have been for me wanting something so badly that I built it for my own use case and then it blew up almost immediately afterwards

principles.text: You don't need to be a visionary; having a real need is enough reason to build.
principles.quote: I'm not the one who built it because I'm some God Dev who figured it out first or some product Visionary that understands what people need better than anyone else I built this for a very simple reason I needed it

principles.text: Everyone has unique needs from their work; any suboptimal part of your life is a software opportunity, whether or not you know how to build it.
principles.quote: you have something in your life that is not optimal right now that a piece of software could make easier it might be software that you know how to write it might be software you don't know how to write what I'm telling you here is it doesn't matter do it

principles.text: Make what you want to exist and make it great; worst case you have something to talk about in interviews.
principles.quote: if you make the things that you want to exist if you make them so good that you genuinely enjoy them you will almost certainly eventually find a lot of success with that in the absolute worst case you have a great thing to nerd out about in your next interview

principles.text: Niche tools beat incumbents by removing friction and unneeded steps; local, in-browser processing means no cloud cost or paywall.
principles.quote: none of these require the cloud I can turn Wi-Fi off of my computer and it will still work exactly the same

principles.text: Even a niche audience will reward a tool that fixes a pain they share; early traction can come quickly without marketing.
principles.quote: the number of YouTubers who have already hit me up saying holy [ __ ] how has nobody made this right before thank you so much

sources.title: Everything we knew about software has changed: think wider, not just bigger
sources.originalTitle: Everything we knew about software has changed — Theo Browne, @t3dotgg ​
sources.summary: Theo argues that each model era (tool calls, long-running tasks, orchestration) shifts what one builder can ship, so old project tiers have dropped a level. Devs must drop skeuomorphic habits and sunk-cost attachments, then build wider across a product's breadth instead of only deeper.

principles.text: Models improve faster than we do, so the move is to build bigger, not to get better at the same work.
principles.quote: The models are getting better faster than we are. So, we can't necessarily get better. So, instead we have to go bigger.

principles.text: Prompt the model to orchestrate and verify; you don't need custom tooling or a software factory to go further.
principles.quote: You don't need some custom tooling, some custom system, some fancy software factory. You just need to prompt it to go a little further.

principles.text: Question habits that exist only because "it's how we've always done it": identity tied to languages, sunk-cost code, guilt merges.
principles.quote: Is this how we do things cuz it's right, or is this how we do things cuz it's just how we've always done it?

principles.text: Project tiers have shifted down one level: yesterday's startup is today's side project, and some products are now just a markdown file on a cron.
principles.quote: Now that the models are bigger, the tiers have shifted. Everything is now one tier lower.

principles.text: Think wider: cover broad range across a category, and let users build missing depth themselves if you architect the product to be extensible.
principles.quote: If you architect your systems and you architect your products in such a way that users can do things that they you never would have guessed.

principles.text: If your idea doesn't feel stupidly ambitious, it isn't big enough.
principles.quote: If your idea doesn't feel stupid, it's cuz your idea's not big enough.

sources.title: How Theo built T3 Chat, the fastest AI chat app, in 5 days with a local-first architecture
sources.originalTitle: My new app is here. It's really fast.
sources.summary: Theo launches T3 Chat and explains why it wins on experience rather than AI: a client-side static app shell, local-first data in IndexedDB via Dexie, and aggressive prefetching. He also covers his low-risk pricing, community-driven roadmap, and why he doesn't fear incumbents copying him.

principles.text: Differentiate on user experience, not on the underlying AI; speed and feel can be the whole product.
principles.quote: we didn't do anything interesting with the AI here what's interesting is the experience we built around it

principles.text: Go local-first and client-side when the app barely needs the server; it removes loading states and feels instant.
principles.quote: when you have an app like this where I just want to navigate click around and do things I don't need the server very often I found that building this way is really really awesome

principles.text: Show stale state instead of loading spinners; cache locally as a backup and let the UI upgrade itself.
principles.quote: there are no loading states there are just stale States

principles.text: Don't over-optimize pricing early; absorb some cost to learn what users actually want before locking tiers.
principles.quote: I didn't want to lock all of this behind us trying to guess and get a perfect pricing model I'll EAD a bit of cost if that's what it takes for us to figure out what is and isn't right

principles.text: Build because you want a better tool; being copied is fine and incumbents rarely execute well when they try.
principles.quote: I didn't build this because I want to be the only person with a chat app everyone uses I built it because I wanted a better chat app

principles.text: Run the roadmap through community feedback and reprioritize quickly when users ask for something else.
principles.quote: I have the features I want to prioritize but I will immediately delay any of them if yall have things you need more

sources.title: Theo on founder mode: stay close to users, hire for what you love, ignore investor advice
sources.originalTitle: We need to talk about "founder mode"
sources.summary: Theo reacts to Paul Graham's "founder mode" essay with lessons from Ping, UploadThing and Twitch. He argues founders should stay hands-on with support and sales, hire only for work they already love, and not take operating advice from investors or manager-style org structures.

principles.text: Don't hire to escape work you dislike; hire for work you love so you must handle the rest yourself.
principles.quote: stop hiring for the things you don't want to do hire for the things you love to do so you're forced to deal with the things you don't want to do

principles.text: Founders should personally do sales and support at ground level, not delegate it early.
principles.quote: I still take all of the sales calls for all of the services we've built it's important to be on that ground level doing support and being involved in these ways

principles.text: Fast, visible bug fixes build more loyalty than never having bugs.
principles.quote: the most loyal users were the ones who had a bug reported it and then we fixed it really fast and told them when it was fixed and thanked them

principles.text: Hiring too early slows a startup; Theo cut the team back to a tiny core to move faster.
principles.quote: Not only was it just more than we needed it was actually slowing us down

principles.text: Don't take operating advice from investors; they rarely give their real reason for passing.
principles.quote: investors will never tell you the real reason they're not investing

principles.text: Impact, not org chart position, should decide who gets access to leadership.
principles.quote: your org chart cannot and should not represent the amount of impact people are having

sources.title: Theo Browne: why a big audience, funding or copycat habits don't build a business
sources.originalTitle: A raw conversation with Theo Browne
sources.summary: Theo Browne argues that success signals (headcount, ad spend, social following) are side effects of real traction, not causes. He covers how T3 Chat grew, why an audience can trap you on the wrong idea, why founder-led social is overrated, and how to hire and learn by doing.

principles.text: Don't copy the side effects of success; they follow real traction, they don't create it.
principles.quote: If your horse isn't moving, doing all of these things to it doesn't make the horse move. It just doesn't work that way.

principles.text: Build what you wish existed; the point is learning and need, not a money plan.
principles.quote: build something that you wish existed.

principles.text: A real startup must be able to scale 100x; niche lifestyle businesses are fine but not venture-scale.
principles.quote: nobody's investing in one of these startups because they want to 2x their money. They're investing because they want to 200x their money 10% of the time.

principles.text: An existing audience gives free early users but can hide a lack of product-market fit.
principles.quote: because you always get those first thousand users, you'll stay on the wrong idea for way too long.

principles.text: Company-run social media rarely works; people follow people, not brands.
principles.quote: people don't watch companies, they watch people.

principles.text: Hire for work you'd miss doing, not work you want to avoid, so you can manage it well.
principles.quote: Hire when you would miss doing it, right?

sources.title: Whole products can now be prompts: Theo Browne on agent-ready codebases, markdown as code and a niche audience
sources.originalTitle: Whole products can now be prompts - Theo Browne
sources.summary: Theo Browne explains why features and even products collapse into prompts and markdown files, and how to build codebases where agents can verify their own work. He also covers using AI to automate only what you understand, and why a deliberately narrow, passionate audience is worth more per viewer to brands.

principles.text: Features and whole products can collapse into prompts or markdown files; prompt before you build tooling.
principles.quote: things that used to be features or even whole products can now literally just be prompts or markdown files.

principles.text: Markdown piped to an agent is now executable, so cron plus a markdown file replaces small services you'd otherwise build and maintain.
principles.quote: The same way I could take a JS file and pipe it to Node and now it executes. I can take a markdown file and pipe it to Claude and it now executes.

principles.text: Write agents a short 'wake-up letter', since they reset every task and only need orientation, not engineering lessons.
principles.quote: agents are incredibly talented engineers experiencing the world's worst Groundhog Day where every time you give them a task, their brain gets reset and they forgot everything they've learned.

principles.text: Raise merge confidence with verification systems; each bump in confidence lets you scale agents and clear backlogs.
principles.quote: That's only possible if you set up your systems so the agents can verify their work well.

principles.text: Automate only what you understand; care deeply first, then use AI on the parts you dislike.
principles.quote: They're not using AI to automate the things they understand. They're using it to avoid building that understanding.

principles.text: Don't widen your audience to chase reach; a narrow, passionate audience is worth more per viewer to brands.
principles.quote: I would also inherently be hurting the value on like a per viewer basis.

sources.title: How Theo built Ping.gg: start from the problem, build primitives, complement OBS
sources.originalTitle: Building Tools for Creators | Theo from Ping.gg | Broman Podcast 151
sources.summary: Theo explains how he went from Minecraft server admin to Twitch tool builder to Ping.gg founder by always starting from a real problem he lived. He covers why paid beats free for quality, why most creator tools target creators who don't exist, and why unopinionated primitives built on open source (OBS) let users invent use cases.

principles.text: Circle around the problem you want solved, not the technology you like using.
principles.quote: i'm entirely circling around the problems i want to solve not the technologies i like to use it's a mistake i see often especially in like the software world

principles.text: Be the user with the pain, or spend hours daily talking to users, before building.
principles.quote: the best way to do that is to be the user with the pain point if you can't do that for some reason then you need to be spending eight hours a day talking to them

principles.text: Talk to target users and ship a rough prototype fast before committing to build.
principles.quote: i made a point to reach out to hosts of multi-person shows on twitch i wrote in like two days a very rough prototype

principles.text: Don't build for creators who don't exist yet; improve workflows for people already creating.
principles.quote: content creation is hard enough that better tools won't make a lot more creators in the same way better ways to start a company don't make more founders

principles.text: Charge for quality instead of racing to free; free tiers can't fund top-tier infrastructure.
principles.quote: there will not be a future where ping is a free product if we want to maintain the quality levels that we're currently like aiming for

principles.text: Build primitives, not opinions; good building blocks let users invent use cases you never imagined.
principles.quote: when you build good primitives you built something that you don't have to think about the use cases as much for because the users can take that primitive and invent things you never would have imagined

sources.title: Why Anthropic hit profitability: multi-cloud distribution, price inflation, enterprise PMF
sources.originalTitle: Holy sh*t I think Anthropic is profitable now
sources.summary: Theo breaks down why Anthropic is reportedly posting its first profitable quarter: availability on every major cloud, quiet price increases via tier shifts and tokenizer changes, API-priced enterprise billing, and one breakout model (Opus 4.5). He argues the profit is partly accidental, because Anthropic under-spent on compute, but the demand is real.

principles.text: Distribution wins: be available in every channel your buyers already use, so choosing you adds no friction.
principles.quote: So, real companies building with AI in their real clouds kind of only had one option and it was Anthropic.

principles.text: Let partners host and resell for a revenue share, so you keep scarce resources for your own priorities.
principles.quote: They put $0 on the line, they give them zero compute, they don't allocate anything, they just send the weights to Google and AWS under crazy agreements

principles.text: Shifting product tiers upward is a stealth price increase that customers accept if the product is good enough.
principles.quote: Opus 4.5 didn't replace Opus 4.1. Opus 4.5 replaced Sonnet. So it's actually a price increase.

principles.text: Revenue compounds: more customers, more usage per customer, and higher cost per task multiply together.
principles.quote: If you double the number of customers, you double their usage, and then you triple their costs, you just 12Xed your revenue.

principles.text: When people love a product they keep paying more, especially when someone else foots the bill.
principles.quote: When people like your models, they will keep using them more, and they will pay basically whatever to do it, especially when they're not the one footing the bill in the end.

principles.text: A real signal of product-market fit is raising prices and watching customers keep spending.
principles.quote: But the craziest thing isn't the cost increases, it's that companies are still paying them. They're not losing customers because the prices went up.

sources.title: Theo Browne on T3 Stack, simple tech and career growth through excitement
sources.originalTitle: Your Fave Dev YouTuber Theo Browne on Getting into TypeScript, Building Dev Tools & Career Growth
sources.summary: Theo explains how the T3 stack grew from a modular set of tools into an accidental brand, and why he resisted shipping a template. He argues that simplicity scales, that excitement rather than content drives career growth, and that AI should speed up learning, not replace thinking.

principles.text: Default to the simplest stack; simple scales far better than people expect.
principles.quote: if there's anything that I want my impact to have on this industry, it is a reset going as far back as possible to simple is best. Simple scales incredibly well.

principles.text: Build modular stacks where every part is swappable or optional, so you only use what the problem needs.
principles.quote: Any one part could be swapped for another solution, or if you don't need any one part, you can just not include it at all.

principles.text: Refuse to ship a template that would push people into overbuilding with tools they don't need.
principles.quote: if I give you a template, you're going to make your blog with Prisma next off. You don't need these things for these problems.

principles.text: Career growth comes from following what excites you, because energy is what carries you through the hard parts.
principles.quote: Career growth doesn't stop because you picked the wrong tech. Career growth stops because you lose the energy to push through those hard parts.

principles.text: Skill comes from struggling and feeling dumb, not from consuming lectures or courses.
principles.quote: You grow via suffering and you grow via feeling really dumb.

principles.text: Use AI to accelerate your own thinking and learning, never to replace it.
principles.quote: If you're replacing your thinking, you're doing it wrong.

sources.title: Jira and Linear are legacy: build the prototype first, then write the spec
sources.originalTitle: Jira and Linear are legacy software
sources.summary: Theo argues issue trackers were built for a human handoff model that AI agents are dissolving. He pushes his "prototype first, spec second" method from Twitch, says role-splitting and long planning no longer make sense with capable models, and sees automations as most valuable to non-developers.

principles.text: Build a quick prototype before writing the spec; the spec written afterward is far more accurate.
principles.quote: Make a first version of the thing, then make the spec, then build it correctly, rather than write a spec assuming you know how it will work, and build it wrong because you were incorrect with the spec

principles.text: A prototype's job is learning scope and testing worth, not shipping faster, but it often ships anyway.
principles.quote: the point of this process wasn't to get the feature out faster. It was to develop a working prototype of it to know what was required to do it and to make a better spec

principles.text: The first version is always flawed; build it to learn, throw it away, then build the good one now that code is cheap.
principles.quote: The first version of software will always be less than ideal. Do it first to figure it out, throw it away, and then make a good version after.

principles.text: Role divisions existed because humans could do only one job; with capable AI they stop making sense.
principles.quote: My hot take is that the way we have broken up all these pieces made sense when humans did it and a given human could only do one of these things.

principles.text: Skip long multi-step planning; let the model build a first pass and use that as the plan.
principles.quote: There's no reason for planning to take hours. There's no reason for planning to fill your entire context.

principles.text: Non-developers adopt automation most readily because developers have trained themselves to skip it.
principles.quote: So, we've kind of trained our brains to ignore the urge to automate things that aren't super useful.

sources.title: Claude Mythos: a model too powerful to release and what it means for software security
sources.originalTitle: Claude Mythos and the end of software
sources.summary: Theo reacts to Anthropic's unreleased Claude Mythos preview and its system card, covering coding benchmark jumps, cybersecurity risk, Project Glasswing, and centralization of intelligence. It is mostly AI news and security commentary, with little durable business or growth insight.

principles.text: Capability that emerges from getting good at code spreads to every domain built on code; security prowess was not trained directly.
principles.quote: The security side seems to be an emergent behavior from getting good at code. They weren't trying to train it to be good at hacking, they were just trying to make it good at code

sources.title: Increase your surface area for luck: ship more, meet more people, be curious and generous
sources.originalTitle: The actual reason you can't get a job
sources.summary: Theo reads and riffs on Kate Lister's article about making your own luck. His thesis: luck is a function of the number of shots on goal and the people around you. Failures compound into learning and connections, and curiosity-driven, generous interactions (not transactional asks) are what open the right doors.

principles.text: Luck is a surface area you can enlarge, not something that just happens to you; it's opportunity plus prep plus number of attempts.
principles.quote: Luck is a thing that occurs, not a thing that you have. And you can increase the surface area for your luck by thinking more carefully about what you're doing and where you spend your time.

principles.text: Build many things; the winner is rarely the one you predicted. Success comes from willingness to fail repeatedly.
principles.quote: Success doesn't come from a lot of wisdom and foresight and genius. Success comes from the willingness to try and fail over and over again.

principles.text: Failures aren't just failures: each attempt gives learning and connections, so odds improve with every run, not just via the count.
principles.quote: a failure isn't just a failure, it's a learning opportunity. So, not only does each failure increase your chance of success because of the basic statistics of running the thing over and over, every additional run by itself has an increase of the chance of success, too.

principles.text: Frequency matters enormously: a 1% shot taken twice a day hits in about two months; twice a week takes most of a year.
principles.quote: If there's a 1% chance that one of these things goes well for you, you do it twice a day, you'll get there in 2 months. If you do it twice a week, you'll probably get there within a year.

principles.text: Approach people with genuine curiosity and give before you take; don't ask for time or jobs, ask something interesting.
principles.quote: Don't ask for time. Ask something interesting and then you'll get time for free.

principles.text: Surround yourself with ambitious peers and build runway (good team, connections, savings) before betting on a startup, since you only get so many shots.
principles.quote: The people around you massively compound the lux surface area.

sources.title: How Theo built an audience and create-t3-app: Twitter for discovery, YouTube for conversion
sources.originalTitle: Open Source Influencers | create-t3-app | The Secret Sauce Podcast
sources.summary: Theo explains the creator funnel (Twitter to discover, YouTube to succeed, Twitch to convert), why persistence beats single viral posts, and how one stack video became create-t3-app, built by community maintainers. He also covers opinionated-but-modular tooling and why community fills a mentorship gap.

principles.text: Match each platform to its funnel role: Twitter discovers, YouTube grows you, Twitch converts committed fans.
principles.quote: youtube is the place to succeed as a creator twitter's the place to get discovered

principles.text: Platforms with many encounters per session are best for finding an audience; bottom-funnel platforms only serve people who already know you.
principles.quote: nobody's going to twitch to find their next favorite streamer they're going there to follow the person that they met at the top of the funnel

principles.text: Followers come from persistence: people follow after seeing many good posts, not the first one.
principles.quote: nobody clicks the follow the first time you have a good tweet they click the follow when this is the 20th good tweet of yours they've seen

principles.text: Effort and payoff differ by platform: low-effort one-liners can blow up on Twitter, while YouTube demands heavy packaging like thumbnails and titles.
principles.quote: twitter is like low effort high discovery youtube is insanely high effort medium discovery decent conversion

principles.text: Know where your product's buyers actually are; streamers don't watch streams, so streaming a creator tool converts poorly even if viewers love it.
principles.quote: streamers don't watch streams and that's a really important thing to know

principles.text: Force users to make the decisions that matter instead of hiding them behind defaults, and comment the code heavily.
principles.quote: now we force you to think about it because those are decisions you have to make

sources.title: Are junior devs screwed? Why trust and visible care now beat resumes for getting a first dev job
sources.originalTitle: Are junior devs screwed?
sources.summary: Theo explains why the junior dev market has flipped: fewer devs are needed per feature, more are available, and AI acts like an extra team member. Getting hired now depends on being genuinely good and building trust publicly, which means doing hard problems yourself, showing your work, and communicating concisely.

principles.text: Dev leverage has flipped: companies can reorg existing staff, so new hires must clear a much higher bar.
principles.quote: That has fully removed our leverage where previously we could kind of just do whatever we wanted

principles.text: Trust is the scarcest hiring commodity; resumes get ranked by how much the hirer trusts you to perform.
principles.quote: I'm ranking these based on how much I trust that you can pull that off.

principles.text: Build trust by showing your work publicly, including what you didn't understand; admitting gaps is itself a signal.
principles.quote: If you're willing to admit that publicly, you're certainly going to be down to admit it to your team.

principles.text: Use AI to deepen understanding, not to dodge the hard parts that make you better.
principles.quote: I'm saying don't use AI tools instead of improving yourself.

principles.text: Embrace feeling dumb and expect things to break; that mindset is what makes you a great engineer.
principles.quote: The key to becoming a great engineer is first and foremost to accept and embrace the fact that you're not a great engineer.

principles.text: Cold outreach should lead with context, show the tiny gap in your understanding, and make a small, low-friction ask.
principles.quote: Start with the context. Give me a simple here's the thing that led me here.

sources.title: Don't Contribute to Open Source: Why Contribution Goals Put the Cart Before the Horse
sources.originalTitle: Don't Contribute to Open Source
sources.summary: Theo argues that beginners who set "make an open source contribution" as a goal get it backwards. Good contributions come from using software, hitting real problems, and filing issues or fixes. He uses Hacktoberfest spam as the cautionary example and says to build things you understand instead.

principles.text: Open source contributions should be a byproduct of using a project, never the goal itself.
principles.quote: good open source contributions don't come from the goal of contributing to open source they come from an understanding of what the project does that you're contributing to

principles.text: Contribute to the project you use, where you hit a real problem, and start with an issue rather than code.
principles.quote: the best project to contribute to is the one that you use you have a problem with and you've looked through the source code and think you might be able to solve it and even then you should be starting with an issue

principles.text: Arbitrary contribution targets create spam: when you set a count goal, people optimize for the count, not quality.
principles.quote: when you set a goal as arbitrary is get four pole requests merged the result isn't people being very careful meticulous with the four PRS they cut

principles.text: Open source maintainers owe newcomers nothing; it's not a free mentorship or free job program.
principles.quote: open source is not a place to go for free mentorship open source is not a place to go to get a free job

principles.text: Well-written, reproducible issues show you're in the trenches and can be worth more than weak PRs.
principles.quote: being able to articulate problems well and show that you are in the trenches you are out here writing code is way more valuable than convincing some repo to accidentally merge one of your weird poll requests

principles.text: The best way to get better at coding is to build things around problems you understand; use that as the starting point for goals.
principles.quote: goals come from things you understand not things you don't start with something you understand be it a video game you play a random app you want to recreate something that you know so you know when it is or isn't working and work backwards from there

sources.title: Engineering management: build trust, protect energy, let engineers fail
sources.originalTitle: Engineering Managers: An Important Conversation
sources.summary: Theo argues good engineering managers act as buffers who set engineers up for success. The core levers are trust, letting people fail safely, protecting team energy, and making it safe to ask dumb questions during onboarding. He uses Luke Lafreniere at LTT as an example of a non-coder leading tech well.

principles.text: Trust is the main thing a manager builds; make every decision with trust in mind.
principles.quote: one of the most important things you can build as a manager is Trust and almost every decision I make as a manager is to help build trust across the companies that I work at

principles.text: Let engineers fail, especially when you know it's coming; it builds trust and capability.
principles.quote: one of the best things you can do as an engineering manager is let your engineers fail especially when you know they're going to fail

principles.text: Team energy beats every other resource; protect and feed the people who bring it.
principles.quote: there is no business goal that isn't accelerated by a team that's energized by the work they're doing

principles.text: Hold strong opinions weakly and listen to anyone who can back theirs up, regardless of seniority.
principles.quote: I'm really big on strong opinions weekly held where someone on the team can strongly commit to a thing

principles.text: Mandate dumb questions for new hires so they stay energized and onboard in days, not months.
principles.quote: I set a minimum number of dumb questions a new teammate has to ask every day for their first couple weeks

principles.text: A manager doesn't need to be the best engineer; translating between tech and the business matters more.
principles.quote: it doesn't always look like somebody who's been coding for 10 years

sources.title: Theo on UploadThing getting cloned: backend-first uploads, no obfuscation, no egress
sources.originalTitle: A YouTuber Stole My Project (And I'm HYPED)
sources.summary: Theo reacts live to a YouTuber who reverse engineered UploadThing and rebuilt it in a day. He explains the architecture (signed S3 policies, direct client-to-S3 uploads, callbacks) and why the backend callback must be the source of truth. He also shows how he treats copycats and open source: celebrate it, don't hide.

principles.text: Make the backend callback the source of truth; never let uploaded files go unlogged in your own system.
principles.quote: you should never have a file be uploaded that you're not logging somewhere in your service or you run the risk of lost files

principles.text: Design the product so users never pay egress: send only metadata to their server, upload files direct to storage.
principles.quote: we don't want you to have to upload the files to your server because then you have to eat the egress for that

principles.text: Enforce limits and validation server-side with signed policies; never trust the client.
principles.quote: you do the server side because you cannot trust the client to do this

principles.text: Open source is more formality than moat; don't bother hiding how your product works.
principles.quote: the source is just there open sourcing's more formality than anything

principles.text: Welcome people who reverse engineer or clone your work; it is validation and free distribution.
principles.quote: somebody reverse engineering our packages to look into how it works is pretty dope

principles.text: Own your misses publicly and plainly when you ship late.
principles.quote: we were late on that and I'll take the L on that for sure

sources.title: Why vague aspirations make bad goals: set specific, deliverable goals as a developer
sources.originalTitle: Your Goals Kinda Suck - LEVEL UP As A Developer
sources.summary: Theo argues that aspirations like "be an engineer," "learn React," or "contribute to open source" are not goals because they have no clear end. Break them down into concrete deliverables you build, tied to problems you care about, and let the aspirations follow. Passion feeds you through the hard parts, and even failed goals make you a better engineer.

principles.text: Aspirations are not goals. Goals need a clear, deliverable end so you know when you've succeeded.
principles.quote: engineers treat aspirations like goals aspirations are not goals aspirations are not a thing you should be working towards goals are the things you should be working towards and goals should have deliverable ends

principles.text: Keep asking questions of a vague aspiration until it becomes a specific thing you can build.
principles.quote: take that top level imaginary goal of i want to learn react and ask yourself more questions until you get to a deliverable thing

principles.text: Build things to learn. Pick projects around problems you personally have, such as a calculator for a game you play.
principles.quote: building goals around specific problems you can solve will make delivering on them significantly easier

principles.text: Don't start from the goal of contributing to open source. Use a project you already care about and contribute when you hit a real problem.
principles.quote: if you start from a point of genuine interest in the project and then contribute it's going to go a lot better than starting with the goal of contributing and then picking a project

principles.text: Pick destinations you're excited about and proud of, so the pain of getting there is worth it and reinforces the result.
principles.quote: the journey sucks way harder if you don't like the destination so pick destinations you're excited about and proud of

principles.text: Detours and abandoned goals still make you a better engineer, and how you talk about failure is a strong hiring signal.
principles.quote: one of the biggest signals i have for a successful engineer is not how many huge things they've built successfully it's how they handle failure

sources.title: How Theo built Twitch's Mod View with inverse portals under a six-month deadline
sources.originalTitle: The Coolest Thing I Ever Built
sources.summary: Theo recounts building Mod View at Twitch, a fully customizable moderator dashboard, with two engineers in six months. He explains the inverse portal pattern that preserved widget state across drag and drop, and credits team care for users and a padded deadline for the outcome.

principles.text: Build tools for users you genuinely care about; shared care is what makes a project succeed.
principles.quote: that's the main reason why this project succeeded because everyone working on it cared and the outfut speaks for itself

principles.text: When rewriting everyone's code is impossible, find a pattern that works around constraints instead (inverse portals to persist state).
principles.quote: we could have went to every team and Rewritten all of the code to work with a single shared State manager we could have done a lot of different things to make this possible but we had a very short deadline

principles.text: Bet early on patterns you already believe in (hooks, functional, composable) and go all in.
principles.quote: we went all in on hooks we went all in on functional programming we went all in on a composable Model to make this possible

principles.text: Build on open source libraries and fork them when they almost fit, rather than starting from scratch.
principles.quote: I ended up internally forking it in order to add all the functionality that we needed on top of that

principles.text: Set the official deadline early to create a buffer month for polish.
principles.quote: I actually had the product manager set the deadline a month early so we would have that extra month in the end to things up

principles.text: Test at the scale of your biggest users to find performance problems before launch.
principles.quote: I had I think six laptops and four desktops all on my desk testing against various really large streams

sources.title: Making Good Tech Decisions: measuring cost, value and risk with ramp-up, maintenance and off-boarding curves
sources.originalTitle: Making Good Tech Decisions - MY FIRST CONFERENCE TALK
sources.summary: Theo's first conference talk gives a framework for picking technology: measure cost (ramp up, maintenance, off-boarding), value, and risk against where the team and business are heading. He compares tRPC, GraphQL, Redwood and create-t3-app to show why modular choices keep the cost of leaving cheap.

principles.text: Treat tech picks like hiring: a big investment and a bet you must plan to maintain or exit.
principles.quote: just like employees tech is a big investment that you make and are to an extent betting on you have to think about the long-term impact of those decisions

principles.text: Break technology cost into ramp up, maintenance over time, and ramp off (off-boarding), since they vary wildly by tool.
principles.quote: i like to break this into three separate sections the ramp up time the maintenance overtime as well as the ramp off time

principles.text: Judge a tech's value by time saved, user wins, developer happiness and hiring impact, not just features.
principles.quote: how much time does this library save us what are the wins that our users will feel from these technologies how much happier are developers

principles.text: Treat risk separately from cost and value; assess your own tolerance for it and plan around it.
principles.quote: risk is something that we don't necessarily know but it's something we can plan around

principles.text: Pick the tool that fits the current stage and accept paying the migration cost later, when growth justifies it.
principles.quote: we have five people working on ping right now it is not that big a deal for us to make it way smoother to get those things out knowing that we can pay this cost in the future

principles.text: Choose modular tools: cheap off-boarding is the easiest way to reduce the risk of any technology bet.
principles.quote: it's also without question the easiest way to reduce the risk of any technology bet that you make

sources.title: Theo on why open source beats a company for freedom and experimentation (OpenClaw meetup Q&A)
sources.originalTitle: OpenClaw meetup Q&A; Peter Steinberger & Theo, OpenClaw inventor & creator of t3 chatwhere
sources.summary: Theo joins Peter Steinberger at an OpenClaw meetup Q&A. He argues running a company with payroll and investors removes freedom, while open source keeps you free to say no and experiment. He also pushes users to donate to the projects they rely on and founders to launch every small ship loudly.

principles.text: Running a company reduces freedom: payroll, benefits and investor expectations lock your day to outside forces.
principles.quote: People seem to think like when you run your own company, you get more freedom somehow. But it's actually the exact opposite.

principles.text: Open source keeps you free: you answer to users, not investors, so you can say no.
principles.quote: Open source is way more freeing even if like you have users that are upset with you. It's a lot more to say no when you have users and not investments

principles.text: External pressure from investors forces a fixed path and shrinks room to experiment, so open source is a safer way to explore.
principles.quote: they have to take a certain path due to external pressures and the opportunity to experiment inherently reduces when that happens.

principles.text: If you rely on an open source project, pay for it: people spend heavily on hardware and AI subscriptions but won't donate a few dollars.
principles.quote: YOU CAN SPEND $700 on a Mac you didn't need. You can't spend $5 a month on the project.

principles.text: Launch every small release publicly; each new app or feature is its own announcement moment with its own users.
principles.quote: You got to like do an announcement for each of these things. You have an iOS app, an iPad OS app, and an Android app. And they all have different users.

sources.title: Theo Browne's $1M+/yr creator-founder setup: a paywalled Indie Hackers teaser

principles.text: Concentrate attention on the channel and the one or two products with momentum; keep older products maintained, not expanded.
principles.quote: I currently focus on my YouTube channel and T3 Tools' products (T3 Chat & T3 Code).

principles.text: Products need not all earn: an open-source free product can build large reach alongside a monetized one.
principles.quote: T3 Code has over 60,000 users in just a few months, but it is open source and not monetized.

principles.text: Revenue concentrates in one product; the others are valuable mainly for reach.
principles.quote: While none of our other products approach T3 Chat's revenue, a few have similar reach.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo walks through his chaotic path: Twitch, a music startup, T3 Tools/Ping, YC, accidental YouTube success, laying off his team after overhiring, and finally T3 Chat. The lesson is that he never predicted the winners, only recognized wrong paths, built things he wanted, and stayed close to users.

chunks.heading: From college to Twitch: how Theo became an engineer worth hiring
chunks.text:
- Theo graduated with music and CS degrees and little to show: one internship he describes as bombed (absent mentor, a 5,400 RPM drive on a $200 laptop) and a Chrome extension, "Chrome Tana", that redirected Bing searches elsewhere.
- He got into Twitch via two people who had unusual faith in him. He bombed the interview but received a 3-month contract, then a 3-month extension, then a full-time offer after he "locked in".
- He credits his manager Waba for functional programming and Elixir, and says that manager "cracked the whip" to make him the engineer he is.
- On the creative team (non-gaming Twitch) he wrote the code for the Bob Ross and Power Rangers marathons and helped start Clips TV.
- The team was two engineers, one manager and about seven partnerships people. Nobody there understood the music/hip-hop world, so he took it over, helped onboard Kenny Beats, and befriended John Wayne (a childhood hero) after offering help in his stream chat.
- The lesson he took: if you reach out to people you look up to "with actual value to bring them", there's a good chance they reply and a good chance they're awesome. He says this shaped how he does everything after.
- From this team he learned to be in the weeds with the people using what he builds, and says he has "never been able to give up" that habit.

chunks.heading: Safety org and the React rewrite: learning to ship inside a big company
chunks.text:
- After the creative org was folded into VOD and he was "thrown overboard", he landed in the safety org, where he had to learn Go (he hated it) and moved into front end.
- He joined as Twitch rewrote its site from Ember to React (the Twilight rebuild, the 2018 beta). He admired a team that rewrote everything from scratch at a ~1,500 person company and succeeded.
- He got good at front end fast, was promoted, helped grow the team from 2 people to about 30, and ran a large number of interviews.
- What he says safety taught him:
  - How to ship inside a moving org.
  - How to fight for users and care about details.
  - How to think full stack.
- He built Mod View, which he names among the things he's most proud of, and talked directly to the moderators using it daily.
- He advises people to "get a normal job" so they can find a team they love, because those connections last. Many of his later successes trace back to people he met in safety, including YC contacts.

chunks.heading: Why he quit Twitch (twice), and the mistake of delaying it
chunks.text:
- In 2020, after Mod View shipped, he moved to the creator team to bring what he learned to the creator dashboard, which he says is still a worse experience than Mod View.
- He calls this a mistake not because of the move, but because it was a way of "delaying a thing I'd already been thinking about, which was quitting". He told himself he'd get promoted within a year, and if not he would finally quit.
- The new org disliked fast shipping because it made them look bad. He says one blocker didn't merge a single PR for three months.
- COVID removed his favorite part of the job: lunch and dinner conversations with smarter, more experienced engineers.
- A colleague (Merryweather) told him he was glad Theo was at Twitch because it showed the early-stage energy wasn't gone. Theo later realized this meant he was bringing startup energy to a company too big, and "I cared more about the users than the company did. And that's never a good place to be in."
- He quit in early 2021. His last day ended with his account being deactivated mid goodbye call.
- He joined a music startup the following Monday, wrote no break into his schedule, and left after a founder fight. He says he wrote the React Native app in 3 days (the contractors had shipped nothing), then rewrote a ~50,000 line backend in ~500 lines with more features. It was blocked for lack of unit tests, so he wrote 600 lines of tests with 100% coverage and handed in his notice with it.
- Pay went from about $475K/year at his Twitch peak, to $125K at the startup, to $0.
- He also says arguing with people who "don't get it" was a skill he had to learn, because at Twitch he had argued with people smarter than him who would hear him out.

chunks.heading: The decision to start a company
chunks.text:
- After quitting he interviewed at Railway (received an offer), Station Head (a music startup that wanted him) and Retool (~10 employees then, 500+ now).
- Alongside, he had a side project: Round (round.t3.gg), a WebRTC tool for collaborative live streaming. A creator had said they'd "pay any amount of money for something that sucks less than Discord".
- It was his first Next.js project (originally Vite on Vercel with an API directory).
- Gun, an ex-Twitch coworker running VShojo (the biggest VTuber org in the West), asked him for one feature, then asked "What do I have to pay you to work on this full-time". Iron Mouse was the first user.
- The decisive pushes: Jake (Railway CEO) said "I see where your heart is. You need to do a startup"; Murray (Station Head) said the same; Bill said it was time.
- He had been avoiding it: he switched teams instead of quitting Twitch, joined another small startup instead of committing to his own, and interviewed widely so he could work on it on the side. He says that hesitation was the pattern, and that he "caved" and incorporated T3 Tools Inc. in September 2021.
- The plan was a suite of creator tools for live and video, "the Adobe suite, but for live video". He says he used to make fun of startup bros and still does, "just with much more ammo".

chunks.heading: Raising money and getting into Y Combinator
chunks.text:
- Seed round: about $300K from "rich homies", with about 15 to 30 people writing $10 to 20K checks, for under 5% of the company. Dax's was the first check to land, Bill's the second, the rest friends from Twitch, old coworkers and college friends at Microsoft and Dropbox. Jake's advice: give a hard deadline to pay the SAFE and cut off anyone who misses it. Jake then missed it.
- Raising from friends was easy, but he says he didn't know how to explain the company to an investor, so he applied to accelerators. South Park Commons rejected him with no feedback; he sent roughly the same application to Y Combinator and got in.
- The application needed a one-minute video. He recounts it as cringe; he was an engineer more than a marketer.
- Michael Seibel interviewed him. His winning answer: "all video is live" until it hits a point where it dies (SD card, transfer, transcode, sort, edit). Make more of the pipeline live and synchronous and production gets more efficient. He still believes it.
- The deal: $125K for 7%, versus the ~5% he had just given up for $300K, so it looked like a bad deal. Michael gave him until 8:00am to decide, calling at 7:50.
- He was up all night. Bill said he trusted Theo but would be "very disappointed" if he said no. Waba, expected to disagree, replied: "You'd be [ __ ] stupid to not take the deal Theo."
- He says YC was one of the best things he ever did. Michael's advice on the call: "You need to find co-founders. You do not want to do this [ __ ] yourself", and Theo convinced his roommate Mark to quit and join on December 31st before the batch (Winter 2022).
- Michael also pushed him, through introductions to broadcast and creator-business people (including the Frame.io founder), toward realizing a product for Twitch streamers was a lost cause.

chunks.heading: YouTube started as a side effect, then outgrew the product
chunks.text:
- He started the channel to explain things he couldn't in Twitter Spaces, not as a career. He was a Twitter-Spaces regular at the time (that's how he met Tanner Linsley and Jacob, and how he found tRPC) and wanted senior dev conversations that didn't exist.
- The T3 stack came from rewriting Jacob's project in two hours to prove the stack. The "T3" name predated Tailwind/tRPC: it came from a Twitch friend's name and a pun on Tier 3 subs.
- A Dan Abramov mock-interview video (done to showcase a good non-LeetCode interview and Ping) blew up the channel, getting ~100K plays. His next video (Solid, Christmas Eve) bombed, which he says broke his heart, so he went all in on YC for three months and posted almost nothing.
- By the end of YC he says he "won the Twitch streamer market" and the reward was about $8K a month: streamers don't spend much, don't stick around, and will use Discord even though it sucks. He had hired six people.
- In April 2022 he went from one video a month to weekly or more, motivated by wanting to nerd out and understand why creators wouldn't use his product. He hit 100K subs in the first year and never expected more than 10K.
- Key realization: "I was more popular than all but like four of our thousandish users." Live streaming wasn't a growth channel, just engagement; his Twitch viewers came from YouTube videos.
- He learned to make "something people want" from YC, and says it's easier if "you are people": build what you deeply want, then compromise to see what others want it for. He cites T3 Chat (voice mode is a thing he'd never use, but users want it).
- Editing his own videos made him better at speaking, copy, branding and fundraising. His hiring advice: "Don't hire for the thing you want to avoid. Hire for the thing you love so you'll go get good at the thing you're avoiding." He edited for about 6 months longer than he should have, and only then hired the right editor.

chunks.heading: The painful part: overhiring, layoffs, and learning not to sell to creators
chunks.text:
- By January 2023 he accepted he "did the startup thing wrong" and was "cosplaying as a big company". He had about 6 employees for roughly a hundred recurring users and about three support questions a day: a support person, two junior engineers, a full-time designer.
- The design polish didn't move conversion: the product's value was how well and reliably it worked. Low-latency video infrastructure was also expensive.
- He laid everyone off, with generous severance and help finding jobs, right before the wider layoff wave. He says he "effectively blown a million dollars" paying people to pretend to be a big company, and that it took about 9 months (April to January) to recognize.
- The realization that triggered the rethink: he was too exhausted by content to adopt a new creator tool himself, so why would creators? His conclusion: "if you're building a tool that's exclusive customer base is creators and influencers, you are going to struggle immensely to even make money, much less be a scalable business." Dev tools are much easier to sell.
- Ping capped around $8K MRR.
- He is now hard on startups that overhire for the same reason.

chunks.heading: Finding the winning product: small tools, then T3 Chat
chunks.text:
- Webhook Thing (replaying webhooks in dev) got little traction. Pick Thing (background removal for thumbnails) became UploadThing after he again got frustrated with S3 setup; the original bucket was still named "P thing".
- UploadThing was the first dev product with real traction beyond the T3 stack, peaking around $12K MRR. He admits much of the adoption was because he was a popular YouTuber, and that the problem "just wasn't big enough or cared about enough". Julius (from the community) started part-time while in college and is now essential.
- He later made Marker Thing (open source, free, used for stream topics → CSV → video chapters) and a real Pick Thing (about $1 to 2K/month with good margins). The business was losing money but he figured four more Pick Things would reach break-even, "default alive" in YC's phrase, at roughly $22 to 25K/month.
- T3 Chat: in December 2024 DeepSeek V3 felt like Claude at under a fiftieth of the price, but its website was broken. He built "Better Chat" over the holidays (Dec 24 to Jan 1), then Mark joined for payments. He found T3.chat available at retail price.
- When V3 slowed from ~180 to 200 tokens/sec to 60 to 70, he found GPT-4o mini on Azure was fast and used YC cloud credits to run it as the default, and charged $8/month for unlimited (Mark's idea, which Theo says helped a ton).
- Results: within about two weeks it made more than the rest of the business combined, and soon after the company was profitable. He won't share revenue numbers because they help investor negotiations.
- He says he expected five products at $2 to 4K/month each, not one that "trounced everything we had built combined". He also got deep into AI quickly by reading reports, following Artificial Analysis and talking to people like Simon, frustrated by AI "grifting".

chunks.heading: What he concludes about building a company
chunks.text:
- "At no point did I correctly predict what was next for us. I could only ever see what wasn't." His path was a series of recognizing the current path was wrong and cutting it off, not predicting the right one.
- His through-line: caring deeply about users, "caring too much about the users of the thing and what experiences they are having", and making stuff that's good that he's proud of.
- The biggest unlock: removing the salary, the boss and the rival. As an employee he fixated on managers, PMs and reorgs as the enemy. After leaving, "the only thing in my way is me". Having nobody to blame, he says, is what changed his life, and success was inevitable as long as he didn't burn out or grow to hate himself.
- His mistakes were his own, and his team suffered for them.
- Today the team is smaller than at YC and smaller than the team he formed at Twitch by an order of magnitude, yet building bigger, more successful things with more users who care more.
- He also wants to correct a misconception: he did not start the company to cash out on YouTube. The company and the product came first, and the channel started as a side effect.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo argues that "AWS is cheaper" claims miss three things: generous free tiers carry small projects a long way, engineer time is the biggest hidden cost, and managed services let you build in ways that cost less to run. His takeaway is that most teams self-hosting need a very good reason, because they are usually spending more.

chunks.heading: Free tiers carry small teams much further than people assume
chunks.text:
- Theo's first argument against "just use AWS" is how long the free tier lasts. He says he has not shipped a service that doesn't fit within Vercel's free tier.
- Most services he recommends have what he calls "disgustingly generous" free tiers.
- PlanetScale free tier: a billion row reads and 10 million row writes per month.
- PlanetScale $30/month plan: 100 billion reads and 50 million writes.
- PlanetScale overage: $1 per billion reads and $1.50 per million writes.
- He says PlanetScale is billed on how many databases you host, not on reads and writes, so scaling databases properly makes them cheap.
- PlanetScale can pass savings on because it makes its money on enterprise scale and by upselling developer experience, not on margin per unit of compute.

chunks.heading: Clerk pricing and why it compares well to other professional auth
chunks.text:
- Theo says Clerk's pricing is similar to other professional solutions like Auth0.
- The free tier has no credit card and unlimited sign-ins, with up to 5,000 monthly active users. A user counts as active only if they visited that month.
- The Hobby tier is $25/month and is not limited to 5,000 users.
- Overage is $0.02 per additional active user on Hobby and $0.05 on the Business tier, which adds more integrated features.
- Each additional employee in the Clerk dashboard costs $20 initially. He says you probably don't need many, since you can share environment variables.
- His summary: the free-tier window is massive and the rest is cheap. The same holds for Upstash and Axiom.

chunks.heading: Engineering time is the real cost of self-managing on AWS
chunks.text:
- Theo says engineers think of their own time as cheap, but it is not.
- He describes AWS problems that took "sometimes days sometimes weeks" and always added long-term maintenance:
  - setting up CI/CD and linking it to GitHub
  - connecting the database and setting up PgBouncer for serverless traffic
  - switching databases between platforms
  - figuring out AppSync and Amplify
- He says he lost "hundreds upon hundreds of hours" to this, which is expensive, and more so if done for a company.
- A complex custom setup also creates job-security-style lock-in: if the person who built it leaves, the company must find someone to maintain "whatever chaos I have set up."
- Saving a few cents a month only matters once the number of units is large enough.

chunks.heading: When rewriting for cost actually makes sense
chunks.text:
- Theo cites other creators' "line of prime": the point where a service is stable in features, high in traffic and predictable in usage, so rewriting it as a stable self-hosted system to minimize cost pays off.
- He says most teams, including those at big companies, are far from that point because most code is still changing and the cost of change is high.
- He would bet that at most companies it costs more to pay engineers to build their own developer experience than to pay Vercel and similar vendors for theirs.
- As a team lead, company owner and investor, he says it matters to understand how valuable engineer time is. Engineers should work on unique business differentiators that make the product better for users and beat competitors.
- Contrast: don't spend a $200k/year engineer's time saving "100 bucks a month" on AWS.

chunks.heading: Scale-to-zero billing makes costs track usage
chunks.text:
- Theo says these services save actual money, not just time, because you are billed when users use the service, not when the month ends.
- Running servers means paying for compute that sits unused, even if Kubernetes and Terraform are set up well.
- With Vercel and PlanetScale, cost flexes with usage across every part of the app, and you don't pay for servers that sit idle.

chunks.heading: Caching, edge functions and HTTP database access cut compute
chunks.text:
- Vercel's cache primitives and incremental static regeneration mean the server only computes when things have changed.
- PlanetScale's database.js package hits an HTTP endpoint instead of opening a SQL connection, so you avoid connection pools and bouncers. It can be called from an edge function.
- Edge function pricing on Vercel Pro: $0.65 per million invocations, and the function only runs if the data isn't already in cache.
- His example: update the posts on a Twitter-style profile only when the user makes a new post, so every other request hits the cache and uses no compute.
- He says it is "so much cheaper to cache a response than to run a server that processes every single request."
- Setting up caching and a CDN yourself returns to the engineer-time cost above.

chunks.heading: Bottom line on hosting your own
chunks.text:
- Theo says he recommended these services before any of them paid him, because they saved him time, money and energy and made it faster to build the right solution for users at every scale he has worked at.
- He argues people who call them too expensive don't see where the cost is.
- His rule: "if you're hosting your own backends and you're hosting your own services you better have a damn good reason because you are costing more money the vast majority of the time."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo built two free, open-source browser tools (SVG to PNG, square image generator) because existing options were slow, paywalled, or lacked basic features. His takeaway: solving your own annoying problem is the most reliable way to find products people want, as with UploadThing, Pick Thing, and his channel itself.

chunks.heading: Theo's trigger for building tools: a problem he personally has
chunks.text:
- Theo builds small tools when he hits a problem that "seems really easy to solve" but the existing solutions are expensive, broken, or both ("charging you money for something that doesn't work").
- His own case: he often has an SVG (a company or framework logo) that he needs as a PNG, because most video editors don't support SVGs even though his graphics editor does.
- He built two free, open source tools out of annoyance. He says he doesn't know how much he'll maintain them: "I wanted to solve the problem that I had and now the problem is solved and I am happy."
- The tools live on a service called Quick Pick (quickpick.t3.gg), with a Square image generator and an SVG to PNG converter.

chunks.heading: What was wrong with the existing SVG to PNG tools
chunks.text:
- One free tool accepted any upload (zips, folders), so finding the actual SVG was annoying. It was slow and could not scale the output. An SVG that declared a small size (a logo at 117 by 24 pixels) came out as a roughly 2 KB blurry PNG. He notes there was no way to say "since SVG is a scalable vector, scale it up a little bit."
- It also offered PNG to SVG, which he calls fundamentally misguided. You can't turn pixels into a vector; tools like Figma embed the PNG as a base64 data blob inside the SVG. Run through a real tracing tool (Affinity), his face became a "weird watercolor pastel" mess. His advice: if you're looking for a PNG to SVG converter, your understanding of both formats is wrong.
- CloudConvert (cloud-based, so it costs them money) lets you raise the width in settings, but after about three conversions it demands a paid subscription.
- Both tools lacked the one-line fix of restricting the file input to SVGs (`accept=svg`).

chunks.heading: How Theo's SVG to PNG tool works
chunks.text:
- It runs entirely in the browser, with roughly 30-40 lines of core logic. It works with Wi-Fi off and needs no cloud.
- UX choices: upload only accepts SVGs, it shows the original resolution and the scaled output resolution, and the saved file name includes the multiplier used. He initially shipped only a custom scale option and planned to add presets.
- Implementation:
  - Parse the SVG string with a `DOMParser`, read the width and height attributes, multiply them by the scale, and serialize it back.
  - Load the scaled SVG as an image (`data:image/svg+xml` with `encodeURIComponent`), draw it to a canvas sized to match, convert the canvas to a PNG data URL, and trigger the download by programmatically clicking an `a` tag. He notes that "there's no download API," only links.
  - He used `useState` instead of a ref for the canvas, because refs gave him stale references.
  - Most of the Square tool's code was AI-generated (Cursor); he wrote the SVG tool himself. He runs React Compiler on the project.
- He logs saves to Plausible, his go-to anonymous analytics provider. In about 12 hours the site got around 1,000 visitors and 207 conversions.
- A community contributor already sent a PR removing his leftover console logs, and he explicitly invites PRs.

chunks.heading: The Square image generator and why it exists
chunks.text:
- Problem: YouTube Community posts crop non-square images, and you can't show the whole image in the preview. Reddit blurs the sides to fit a square, but YouTube does not.
- Fix: take any non-square image, pad it to a square with a white or black background, and save. He uses it for memes (for example from r/ProgrammerHumor) in his Community posts.
- The existing tool he used before had several friction points:
  - It defaulted to a hard-to-justify red background.
  - It used a blur-hash background that "literally never ever works."
  - It needed about three times more clicks than necessary, with no way to switch images without refreshing.
- His design choices: the background defaults to white (the right default), black is one click, saving is one click without scrolling, and you can cancel.
- YouTubers have told him they were amazed nobody had built this before.
- Remaining to-dos he listed: drag and drop (the label wraps the input, so it needs a fix), more options, a bulk processor, and a favicon generator that people asked for.

chunks.heading: The takeaway: build what you need
chunks.text:
- Theo's main point is that he is not a "God Dev" or a "product visionary." He built these because he needed them. Plenty of developers could have built the same thing.
- "Everyone has unique needs based on the things that they do." Whatever is not optimal in your life, a piece of software could make it easier, whether or not you know how to write it yet. His advice: do it.
- His track record backs the pattern: "some of the most successful things I have built have been for me wanting something so badly that I built it for my own use case and then it blew up almost immediately afterwards." Examples he names are UploadThing, Pick Thing, Quick Pick, his work at Twitch, Ping.gg, and the YouTube channel itself.
- The channel exists because he wanted a senior-plus, conversational deep dive into tech and nobody had made one.
- His claim: if you make the thing you want to exist and make it good enough that you genuinely enjoy it, you will almost certainly eventually find success. In the worst case you have a great thing to talk about in your next interview.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo argues that each model era (tool calls, long-running tasks, orchestration) shifts what one builder can ship, so old project tiers have dropped a level. Devs must drop skeuomorphic habits and sunk-cost attachments, then build wider across a product's breadth instead of only deeper.

chunks.heading: The model eras and why Theo says to build bigger
chunks.text:
- Theo describes three "eras" by model. Sonnet 3.5 is the tool-call era: the first model to call tools consistently enough for day-to-day coding in a real code base.
- Opus 4.5 is the long-running-task era. It could test its own work and finish tasks that take hours instead of minutes. He dates the start of his own "AI psychosis" to November and December of last year.
- Mythos is the orchestration era. He says it's the first model that "understands itself": it spawns additional models, breaks up work, and verifies it afterwards.
- This needs no custom tooling or "fancy software factory". You just prompt the model to go further.
- His conclusion: "we need to go bigger." Most of his old Jira tickets could be solved by Opus 4.5, so his previous work would not benefit from a model like Mythos.
- He admits he was wrong when he claimed models were hitting a wall. Models are improving faster than people are, so people can't just get better; they have to go bigger.

chunks.heading: Software's skeuomorphic phase and the iOS 7 analogy
chunks.text:
- Theo compares today's developer habits to pre-iOS 7 design. The compass app looked like a compass, and the books app looked like a bookshelf with turning pages, because apps had to convince people they could replace physical tools.
- iOS 7 marked the shift from convincing to embracing. The result was a more useful interface: a clear red block for being off-direction and a large heading number.
- He argues developers are in their own skeuomorphic phase. We pretend terminals are the ultimate interface "when they're not even good interfaces", and he says this as someone who deeply loves his terminal.
- "Natural language has no place in a terminal, but we pretend it does because the terminal's familiar."
- Developers care deeply about tools, frameworks and languages, and have "blinded ourselves" into thinking it all matters.

chunks.heading: Habits and identity developers need to drop
chunks.text:
- Theo asks whether we do things "cuz it's right, or is this how we do things cuz it's just how we've always done it?"
- Example: why can't we commit environment files? Sharing one file across a team requires building a separate system, only because Git was built for a specific purpose and took over our heads.
- Identity by language ("I write JavaScript") is not just a junior habit. Senior engineers do it too ("He's not a real developer"). He says these facts "matter less now" and never mattered as much as people thought.
- Developers got away with it because hiring was so hard that companies couldn't push back.
- Sunk cost: people are scared of deleting code, and teams "guilt merge" PRs that took someone a week or two even when the solution isn't right. He argues that when code is cheap, the solution is often to delete and reset.

chunks.heading: Every project tier has shifted down one level
chunks.text:
- Theo's three examples: a Reddit meme scraper (2-3 days, scrapes top posts from programming humor into a copy-paste format), Ping (a Y Combinator startup for high-quality live-creator collaboration inside OBS, built in 2021), and a "full stack cloud" like Vercel with auth and databases built in (current work).
- His old categories: side project, startup, "too big". Now "everything is now one tier lower": what used to be a startup is now a side project.
- Some startups at the event "could have arguably been a side project", and a new tier below side project is "the G brain tier": a markdown file.
- "The fact that you can now execute markdown by just piping it to Codex or Claude is unbelievable."
- Opportunity: build a very small, specific service as a markdown file run on a cron.

chunks.heading: Markdown-plus-cron example
chunks.text:
- Theo had a service to triage and prioritize his PRs with AI review. It is now a markdown file.
- The prompt says: go to these four GitHub repos, look at all open PRs, work out the current status, help prioritize, then update a static HTML file, send it to S3 and give him the URL.
- It runs on a cron at 9:00 a.m., and around 9:15 to 9:20 he has his work for the day.
- He urges the audience to try it, saying many services can be "literally just a markdown file running on a cron".

chunks.heading: Think wider: breadth vs depth
chunks.text:
- Theo says "bigger" is the wrong word; it's time to "think wider". Software has breadth (range of things covered) and depth (features within an area).
- Vercel doesn't have all of AWS's features and never will, but it goes deeper in full-stack, front-end-leaning servers. Frontend developers not using it "are feeling some amount of pain", and "even the agents prefer it".
- Historically a startup competing with AWS could never match its range without thousands of engineers. Now that range is viable.
- His claim is not that you can build something as reliable as RDS, but that you can build a database platform into your product in "a day or two of work with enough prompting and enough effort".
- Aim for enough breadth that most users can at least start trying the product. When they need a feature in a vertical you don't support, "it's not your problem" if you've architected the product so users can build the missing features themselves.
- Slack is his example: it "sucks" as a product, but it's now where people run their agents half the time, because it's "the right shape" for building features through its somewhat functional bot APIs.

chunks.heading: Pick ideas that feel stupid
chunks.text:
- Theo's closing message: compete with Slack, build your own AWS, challenge Salesforce directly.
- "If your idea doesn't feel stupid, it's cuz your idea's not big enough."
- He admits he doesn't know what "too big" means anymore (training your own model, your own operating system, competing with NPM and Node?), and says he needs to keep pushing himself bigger than makes sense to find the limits.
- He is working on the full-stack cloud himself and says not to compete with him on that one.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo launches T3 Chat and explains why it wins on experience rather than AI: a client-side static app shell, local-first data in IndexedDB via Dexie, and aggressive prefetching. He also covers his low-risk pricing, community-driven roadmap, and why he doesn't fear incumbents copying him.

chunks.heading: T3 Chat: speed as the product
chunks.text:
