- Cadence changes the timeline: 2 attempts per day reaches that point in about 45 days; 2 per week takes about 45 weeks (315 days), and realistically longer because weeks get skipped.
- Failures are not pure loss. They teach you, make you friends and connections, and show you which markets are cursed, so each additional attempt also has a higher success chance than the last.
- "Trying" is not only building new apps. It is making connections, talking to people, going to events and spending time in the right circles.

chunks.heading: His own failure history before T3 Chat
chunks.text:
- Products before T3 Chat: Ping (capped early; he had to lay off most of the team, "one of the saddest and hardest things I've ever had to do"), a webhook product (a couple of loyal users, never a real business), other creator tools, Marker Thing, and Pick Thing.
- UploadThing came from realizing, while building Pick Thing, that upload was the slowest part. It got heavy package adoption and users abused the free tier, but it made no real money.
- T3 Chat was not the one he expected. He would tell people "why would you build a chat app right now? That's stupid." He built it as one of several small-to-medium projects meant to make a couple thousand a month and keep Ping from running out of money. It became profitable within a month.
- He attributes the outcome partly to luck: people wanting all models in one place cheaply, a genuinely good app, his audience, and things he doesn't fully understand. He argues UploadThing and Ping are arguably better products, so quality alone does not decide it.
- He says "I got lucky, but I got lucky after getting unlucky working harder on other things for years," and expects more future products to fail.
- He rejects the "he stopped building for devs" take: Ping and Pick Thing were both dev products.
- Offer mentioned: T3 Chat is $8/month with every relevant model, and a promo code gave the first month for $1.

chunks.heading: Build runway first, then place bets
chunks.text:
- Theo admits his own surface area was large: college friends, rich ex-Twitch coworkers, low expenses, no kids, and money saved after his job. That let him take repeated risks. He calls this a privilege.
- His response to people who lack this: don't complain about missing runway, build it. Get a decent job on a good team (he says to optimize early career around good teams), network at a boot camp, save enough to coast for 6 months.
- If you only get to place one bet and it fails (and "nobody gets it right the first try"), you have nothing to fall back on. A 1% chance for him may be 2% for you, but "you're still going to die if you have one roll."
- His own path took about 5 years of working before the startup, and he says a 4-year job to build the position isn't a big difference.
- He thinks starting a startup before you have the surface area is probably not the right move yet.

chunks.heading: Peers, college and where you spend time
chunks.text:
- Peers set your pace. His analogy: marathon runners swap pacers so they can focus on the hard part, not on holding speed.
- He pushes college even if you drop out or skip the paper: the value is being surrounded by people to pace against and learn from, and getting better at making connections.
- His early investors came from college contacts and his first job, which let him raise enough to quit and start the company. Those connections also got him into YC after rejections from easier accelerators, and then "I failed for 4 years."
- Avoid peers who blame the world or have shipped the same codebase for eight years without growing. Optimize for the agility you want in your own life.
- A lucky chain example: posting in college Facebook hacking groups led to a friend of a friend who knew Saurik (creator of Cydia), who is now a close friend who has helped him through rough situations.
- He mentions living in San Francisco as another surface-area lever, without elaborating.
- He agrees with the heuristic that someone meeting 1-2 interesting people a day is a good bet; 1-2 a week is too slow to reach escape velocity.

chunks.heading: Don't use shortcuts like open source or fame as a job strategy
chunks.text:
- He says the mindset matters more than a checklist: "what matters here is how you think, not what you do."
- Open source: contributing in order to get a job is cart-before-horse. Good developers end up contributing because they use the tools and fix real problems; the contribution is evidence of that, not the cause of the job.
- Same ordering error: thinking YC acceptance guarantees a startup, or YouTube/Twitter popularity makes people care about what you build. He says people care about what he does because he made it worth caring about, not the reverse.
- Being popular does not mean people care about everything you do; he cites posting music on his tech-heavy Twitter.

chunks.heading: How to build connections: curiosity, giving first, and being useful
chunks.text:
- Approach with genuine curiosity, not extraction. "Don't hit me up because you want something from me. Hit me up because you're curious about something I'm also curious about."
- Don't open with "can I get your time" and a calendar link. Ask something interesting and "you'll get time for free." Same logic in fundraising: ask for advice and people offer money; ask for money and you get less.
- Example: a thumbnail critique with a redesign, or a thoughtful question about a post, will get a reply from him, whereas "I need a job" cold asks get blocked. He applies the same to Ryan Carniato: a deep question about a post gets a stream rant, a job ask gets silence.
- Friendships he lists that began from shared interests: Sasha Gray (speakers and audio gear), Luke from LTT (phones), and smaller YouTubers he DM'd to help with audio.
- Give before you take: he says he works to make everyone around him feel they get more than they give, because his team can't make what he makes since the channel and business are his.
- Be useful before asking. A developer first appeared by dropping a useful Zen/Excalidraw hotkey extension in his chat; when that person later said he was starting a company, Theo's first response was to ask if he could invest and "write the check."
- He reframes "don't meet your heroes": meet them, but arrive to thank them or help, not to ask. He's met nearly all his skateboarding heroes, including Tony Hawk, and says it's been great.
- Generosity can take the form of attention (responsive), time, or resources.

chunks.heading: Concrete examples of surface area paying off
chunks.text:
- The best "I need a job" DM he's received (from Sahaj, creator of Tweakcn): four sentences, a clear diagram of strengths (DevOps on one side, design on the other), the type of role, and a remote preference. Theo posted it publicly with "Hire him"; eleven days later Sahaj joined v0 at Vercel. Theo credits Sahaj's own communication, not his referral.
- SnitchBench: he re-recorded the video four times and automated the benchmark after realizing it deserved building properly. The benchmark became more relevant than the video, led to connections including Simon Willison, and Theo plans to forward half his sponsors to Simon since Simon earns almost nothing from his blog.
- Student at a college event: asked him on the spot to speak at their school after noting he likes Waterloo students; Theo said yes because he wanted more Waterloo students to know him, and says he has never made a bad hire or investment from a Waterloo student.
- Advent of Code: competing on the leaderboard turned a chatter, Chris, into a moderator and friend who got him to record a talk for his college.
- Putting two people together: he brought a ten-year college friend, Von, to SF and into his friend circle, which he calls his favorite thing to do.
- Acting like a bigger role: behave like the Michelin chef covering a brunch shift; people notice effort that wasn't strictly required.

chunks.heading: Writing, events and tolerating awkwardness
chunks.text:
- Share your genuine thoughts online. The writing needn't be original or literary, just reflect your real interests. Theo says a blog is among the first things he'd do with no professional connections, noting the author's Substack has helped her hiring.
- Don't change topic to chase audience; share what excites you with others who care. Example DM that works: "you said X in a video, I thought about it so much I wrote this post."
- Hosting events: he doesn't do it himself and finds it socially draining, but sees a pattern where being the place a group meets works. His "Theo orbiter" SF group runs its own Discord and Friday events without him.
- Suggestions from the article: coffee, a stoop meetup, pizza. Monthly bagel brunch is cheap, low-stakes and rarely competes with other plans. If others want a thing and you initiate it, you win even if it fails because you learn demand.
- Expect to feel socially flailing and awkward at the start (he felt awkward in his first programming Twitter Spaces and now talks to rooms of 800 without a thought).
- Don't judge people from outside: he is often assumed to be a "drama farmer" but says he quietly defuses far more drama than he covers, and that people he helped defend him. Let assumptions be corrected quickly by new information.
- Showing up and being accessible leads to unpredictable loops: trying to calm the WordPress drama led to an invite to Matt Mullenweg's birthday party and meeting Joshua, creator of Delicious.
- His bottom line: "There is no growth hack that is more powerful than talking about the stuff you care about with others who also care about the thing."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo explains the creator funnel (Twitter to discover, YouTube to succeed, Twitch to convert), why persistence beats single viral posts, and how one stack video became create-t3-app, built by community maintainers. He also covers opinionated-but-modular tooling and why community fills a mentorship gap.

chunks.heading: Building a full-stack TypeScript stack around type safety and modularity
chunks.text:
Theo's core engineering pitch is full-stack type safety so teams of any size can build safe applications as fast as possible.

- His stack: PlanetScale (database), Prisma (database connection layer), Tailwind (UI), TypeScript, Next.js with React, and tRPC to bind back end to front end.
- He did Advent of Code in full strict TypeScript, "not a single any" for three years, and regularly breaks the top 100.
- His view: "You move faster when you let type safety carry you." You stop double and triple checking everything and trust the compiler.
- With tRPC, his router, queries and mutations contain no explicit type definitions: "you don't need to write TypeScript to benefit from TypeScript if your system infers from value to user."
- He says tRPC takes about an hour to set up vanilla and immediately saves time and fixes bugs.
- He insists every piece of the stack is swappable and carries little buy-in to any one part. He had swapped into each piece from other tools.

chunks.heading: Why Tailwind is closer to TypeScript than Bootstrap
chunks.text:
Theo defends Tailwind as a productivity layer over CSS, not a prescribed UI kit.

- Bootstrap is "closer to Angular": a prescribed way to do UI that prevents you from writing the CSS. Tailwind is closer to TypeScript or CoffeeScript: an extension that makes CSS faster to write.
- Hovering a Tailwind class in the editor shows the one line of CSS it applies. Only about four class types add more than one line.
- Using it with a cheat sheet makes you better at CSS. On projects without Tailwind he is in the Tailwind docs more, because he trusts it and knows what it does.
- He didn't like writing CSS before Tailwind. His designer loves it too, and an engineer and a designer agreeing means "you actually struck gold."
- His line: Tailwind makes inline styles pleasant and maintainable. His opinion: "if you're not using it you need a good reason."

chunks.heading: How create-t3-app happened from one stream
chunks.text:
The most successful open source project around Theo came from a video, not from code he wrote.

- He streamed building a "roundest Pokemon" voting app from scratch in about an hour and a half with his stack. The VOD sat unwatched, then reached about 150,000 plays on YouTube, the best performer on his channel besides the Dan Abramov interview.
- People kept asking for a boilerplate repo. He refused at first: "you don't need to install NextAuth on your blog," and he feared people would use it for things it's not for.
- He floated a CLI that lets you pick technologies and told the community anyone who wanted to build it had his blessing. A teenager from India took the challenge, built it, and became lead maintainer.
- Theo's only contribution is the README. Within about three months the repo had 5,000+ GitHub stars and 50+ contributors, over half first-time contributors.
- His claim: whoever builds the thing that displaces Next.js or React "will have come from my community."

chunks.heading: Opinionated defaults versus developer agency in a starter template
chunks.text:
Theo explains how the team decides what create-t3-app includes.

- Rule: only bake in decisions that matter to everybody. Leave decisions that depend on the app (such as protected route flows) to the developer.
- Env vars are type-safe and validated at build time. A fresh project with all options checked intentionally fails to build until you choose a database and NextAuth credentials.
- Earlier versions shipped a default SQLite database. People didn't know they could change it or that it wasn't suited to production, so the template now forces the choice.
- This is the source of many support requests but also a funnel: forced confrontation produces questions, then Discord, then contributions.
- "Create T3 App was not built to make you feel smart, it's built to let you be dumb."
- He heavily comments the decisions the template makes.

chunks.heading: The creator funnel: where to discover, build, and convert an audience
chunks.text:
Theo's model for how creators move viewers across platforms.

- Top of funnel (Twitter, TikTok): many people per session, short engagement. Best place to be discovered. Bottom of funnel (Twitch, Patreon, OnlyFans): nobody goes there to find someone new; they follow someone they met higher up and convert into spenders.
- YouTube is the middle: algorithmic discovery exists but is a harder fight to get into the feed.
- His summary: Twitter is low effort and high discovery. YouTube is insanely high effort, medium discovery, decent conversion. Twitch is the bottom of the funnel. "YouTube is the place to succeed as a creator, Twitter's the place to get discovered."
- One-sentence Tailwind tweets blew up on Twitter. On YouTube he spends hours on editing, thumbnail and title, then watches the first two hours and adjusts the thumbnail and title if click-through is weak.
- His own streaming doesn't convert for Ping: "streamers don't watch streams." YouTube viewers convert much better.
- The Twitch stream is still valuable for recruiting. He says he'll never struggle to find a good engineer to hire, and that if he built developer tools he'd be "very wealthy" but wants to solve creator problems.

chunks.heading: Growing on Twitter and building a community through persistence and content
chunks.text:
How Theo grew an audience and a community.

- Persistence is the driver: "nobody clicks the follow the first time you have a good tweet... when this is the 20th good tweet of yours they've seen, they're like oh fine I'll follow this guy."
- His early growth came from showing up in other people's streams and Spaces. A Tanner Linsley Space gave him "homework" (look into tRPC and Blitz) and then an audience for the follow-up conversation.
- After a YC period, his Twitter went from about 4 followers a month to about 6,000 in one month once he engaged again.
- Editing his own videos made him stream better: more focused topics, more cohesive ideas, asking chat for feedback.
- He started his Discord, about 4,000 people, because he lost his 300-plus person front-end Slack channel after leaving. It attracts people who lack mentorship or peers at work.
- It serves skilled self-taught devs with deep technical ability who are "beginner exclusively in career" and have no place to land.
- His advice on open source contribution: it happens when you find real problems while using lots of open source, then fix and ask the maintainer. "Engineers suck at setting goals"; "I want to contribute to open source" is an identity, not a goal.

chunks.heading: How Ping began: networking, mentorship, and founder fit
chunks.text:
Theo's route to founding Ping (now Ping.gg).

- He left Twitch because roles there didn't focus enough on creators, joined another startup that wasn't a good fit, and realized he could build his own thing.
- Railway CEO Jake recruited him, he passed the interviews, but Jake saw his heart was in Ping and pushed him to do it. Jake introduced him to co-founder Brendan Hawker, a product and design person.
- He credits relationships with other developers for compounding value and says he tripled down on them.
- Product: tools for creators to bring guests on streams and videos with professional quality, built on WebRTC.
- Latency claims: under 100 ms regularly from San Francisco to Japan versus about 2 seconds best case for Twitch (down from 15). He cites about 16 ms per frame in 60 fps games and roughly 35 to 50 ms for synchronized music.
- Brand: the name Ping came from a collaborative naming session; he got ping.gg and reclaimed t3.gg for himself after the company previously used the T3 brand ("Roundest by T3 Tools", "Ping Labs").

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo explains why the junior dev market has flipped: fewer devs are needed per feature, more are available, and AI acts like an extra team member. Getting hired now depends on being genuinely good and building trust publicly, which means doing hard problems yourself, showing your work, and communicating concisely.

chunks.heading: Why the junior dev market is harder now: leverage and team size
chunks.text:
Theo frames the hiring market with three axes: devs needed per feature, devs available to hire, and money available to hire them. For years these trended in developers' favor. He argues that is no longer true.

- Devs needed per feature has slowly fallen, helped by better tools, lower product expectations, shipping faster for earlier feedback, and AI.
- Devs available has risen much faster, and money to hire them has dropped.
- The gap between "engineers needed" and "engineers available" is leverage. It used to favor engineers so strongly that companies hired people just so competitors couldn't (he cites Facebook hiring web framework creators).
- Now he says a company is more likely to reorg existing staff, or lay people off, than hire new people.

His example: the Twitch Mod View team (about 2020-2021) needed five people. Two were already on the team, one was moved over from another team, one was an intern converted to full-time, and one was poached from another company (he believes Disney Plus). Roles got hundreds of applications. Building the same thing today, he says, two of those roles would simply not exist, and the team might be two people plus AI, which he calls "person 3.5 Claude". Where does a junior fit on that team? "They don't fit and it sucks."

chunks.heading: Hard problems build skill, and AI is the easy out
chunks.text:
Theo says juniors improve by leaving the layer they are stuck in. Before AI, he had to isolate a problem, search, then ask his manager, who would often reframe it entirely ("Why are you rendering that element at all?"). The common junior mistake is staying stuck on the console error when the problem lives a layer higher.

- Humans instinctively avoid hard, painful things, so "Claude, fix this error" is the easy out.
- Becoming a great engineer means accepting you are not one yet and being willing to feel stupid constantly. "Feeling dumb becomes the best feeling once you learn to embrace it."
- He learned this from skateboarding: you improve by hitting the ground, so you go in expecting to fall, which makes landing it feel magical.
- When building, expect the code not to work, so reduce the number of moving parts so any single failure is easy to identify, fix and replace.
- He relies heavily on Cursor himself, but says it works for him because his brain was already wired to solve hard problems.

chunks.heading: Compensation is a step function, so trust is the scarce resource
chunks.text:
Theo argues that developer pay is not a smooth upward curve. In the US it is zero until you cross a quality bar, then jumps. His line: "If you're not worth $100,000 a year as a software dev in the US, you're worth zero dollars a year as a software dev in the US."

- Previously the shortage of devs lowered that bar, and companies bet on lower-tier hires hoping they'd be promotable in 2-3 years. He says that investment no longer makes sense.
- Being good enough is not sufficient without trust. When he reviews a stack of resumes, he ranks by how much he trusts the person to perform, not by school or resume content.
- In the Mod View example, he trusted the existing teammates, the transferred employee (visible commits), the intern (paid a small amount to prove themselves) and the poached hire (proven record elsewhere).
- In a market of 500 to 5,000 AI-generated applications, you can't win by being slop application number 5,001.

chunks.heading: How to build trust and stand out
chunks.text:
Theo says the way to beat the bar is to grow in public and show you care.

- Show your work: write a blog post on two solutions you tried and what you liked and didn't. Admitting "I didn't understand this part" is a good signal, because it shows you'll tell the team when you don't know something.
- Seniors can quickly tell whether you understand what you're writing about. He saw two Twitch candidates whose "React site" was a pasted HTML template in a single component with no state or logic.
- Be present in communities where people care about the same things; his own team formed from people who hung out in the same places and showed that care.
- Don't buy a resume course, pad commit counts with AI-generated repos, or spam open source with low-quality PRs. He has a separate video arguing open source contribution isn't the key to a job.
- Useful open source: file a detailed issue with a reproduction (for example a StackBlitz link), then offer a PR to fix it.
- Aim to talk with people at higher salary levels about things they own. At Twitch he found himself mostly talking with people making twice his pay because he was interested in what they built.
- Some capable people are insecure and don't realize their level; working publicly lets them compare themselves and get noticed.

chunks.heading: How to reach out to senior people
chunks.text:
Theo says clear, concise, relevant communication is rare and gets people hired.

- Bad DM: a life story, several paragraphs, then a vague "what do you think?" It is unclear why you picked him, and it reads like you think he is rich or can hand you a job.
- Good DM: context first ("In your video about X, I noticed you did Y"), then the specific point of confusion, then a tiny ask such as a resource, not personal teaching. "I will remember you if this is how you DM me."
- Treat senior people as a last-resort resource: use their public content, solve what you can, then ask a small, calm question.
- Even better, follow up with proof of effort (a blog post about what you struggled with) or bring a solution to a problem he has. He cites a developer who sent three sentences and a link to a plugin that formats TypeScript errors prettily; he installed it, made a video, and has sent him job opportunities since.
- He hired a community member for video review and info-gathering because she was concise and dropped useful links rather than essays. He later paid another helper, Gabriel, and referred him to a better job.
- He learned this on Minecraft plugin forums: a specific error, steps tried, and a clear ask got responses (and led him to contribute to WorldGuard).

chunks.heading: What Theo says he is not saying
chunks.text:
He adds clarifications about the advice:

- He is not saying avoid AI. Use it to improve understanding (for example, explain React rendering by comparison to Unreal Engine rendering), or to handle problems you already know how to solve. Don't use it instead of improving. If you can't find the balance, drop the tools and revisit later.
- He is not saying give up. Impact can come quickly once in; he points to shadcn, who he believes had no full-time engineering job before Vercel.
- He is not saying GitHub is worthless, or that you must learn React. Half the people he hired weren't React engineers.
- He is not saying spam famous people with questions.
- His bottom line: it is a better time than ever to be an engineer if you care and a miserable time if you don't, and "trust is a rare commodity nowadays." He would hire a junior who shows a year of growth and asks great questions over a more experienced dev he doesn't trust.

chunks.heading: Theo's own start, and the old path being closed
chunks.text:
Theo says he was not qualified for his first dev job. He got a three-month contract because the manager liked him (including his music taste) and he had a few projects. The contract was renewed once rather than converted, and the following six months were the hardest he has worked and where he became qualified.

- He says the route he used, throwing a resume at enough companies that one was desperate enough to hire him, is closed.
- A company now has 10 qualified applicants per role, so betting on an unqualified person and training them is not worth it.
- It may take longer: he suggests hanging out in communities for two years after college while doing a part-time gig, but "you will make it" if you care enough and keep going.
- He got into code through hosting Minecraft servers, and says motivation should come from love of the craft or curiosity, not just from wanting the salary.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo argues that beginners who set "make an open source contribution" as a goal get it backwards. Good contributions come from using software, hitting real problems, and filing issues or fixes. He uses Hacktoberfest spam as the cautionary example and says to build things you understand instead.

chunks.heading: Open source contributions should be a byproduct, not a goal
chunks.text:
- Theo says most developers shouldn't set "contribute to open source" as a goal. His position is that open source is great, but pursuing contributions as a career hack is the wrong approach.
- He was prompted by a Reddit post from a beginner who wanted a good-first-issue React repo without TypeScript, writing "as I need to start doing open source". Theo's objection: "nobody needs to start doing open source."
- His framing is "cart before the horse". The horse is having a real problem with software you use. The cart is the issue or fix you create for that problem.
- Open source is "about sharing contributions to things you use so others can use them", not a way to get started in development.
- He says that if you can't figure out which projects to contribute to, you shouldn't be contributing yet.

chunks.heading: What open source is not (mentorship, free jobs)
chunks.text:
- Open source is not a place for free mentorship or a free job. Theo calls it "an ecosystem of people working really hard to keep the web and all of software development alive".
- Maintainers are already struggling under the weight of issues, PRs and noise, now including AI-generated pull requests.
- A new developer with an empty GitHub account sending PRs of not-yet-great code mostly frustrates maintainers and wastes their own time.
- Telling new developers they'll get mentorship and jobs from open source is, in his words, "incredibly toxic", and he says it could damage open source if recommended carelessly.
- Mentorship can still happen. Theo has mentored contributors on create-t3-app and UploadThing.
- create-t3-app has over roughly 300 contributors, about half of them first-time open source contributors. He credits that to people who used the project, hit problems, or saw issues they knew how to solve.

chunks.heading: How to contribute well
chunks.text:
- Best project to contribute to: one you use, that has a problem you've hit, where you've read the source and think you can fix it.
- Start with an issue, not with a pile of code you hope someone will mentor you through.
- A well-written issue with detailed reproduction steps is "huge". Theo says articulating problems well shows you're "in the trenches" and is more valuable than getting a weird PR accidentally merged.
- Good contributions come from understanding what the project does, not from the goal of contributing.

chunks.heading: Why open source helps hiring (and why the shortcut fails)
chunks.text:
- As a hiring manager, Theo values seeing real contributions on someone's GitHub. Reading the code builds trust he couldn't get without having worked with the person.
- The contributions are valuable because they show you ran into real problems, fixed them, and took part in the community, not because they exist.
- Treating the contribution as the trophy skips the part that actually carries signal.

chunks.heading: Hacktoberfest as the origin of the problem
chunks.text:
- Hacktoberfest started in 2013 as a DigitalOcean and GitHub collaboration, before Microsoft owned GitHub. Participants made at least four PRs in October to earn a limited-edition t-shirt, with a few hundred participants in year one.
- Theo says the idea was fine at small scale, but the arbitrary "four merged PRs" target led to spam: single-line fixes, grammar opinions, and PR floods to hit the threshold.
- By 2020 maintainers were fed up. He quotes a maintainer calling Hacktoberfest "a corporate sponsored distributed denial of service attack against the open source maintainer community".
- That maintainer reported closing 11 spam PRs in a day on one repo with 485 watchers, at a rate of about 4 per hour before October had even started.
- A Twitter account, "toober fest", documented the worst PRs, such as "please accept my request I will get a free t-shirt".
- His takeaway: telling people who don't understand open source that it's a magic route to a t-shirt or a job produces nonsense.

chunks.heading: Better path: build things you understand
chunks.text:
- Theo's constant advice: the best way to get better at coding is to code more, building and solving problems you understand.
- Examples he gives: a web app tracking what you mine in Minecraft, or a site tracking your favorite sports team's scores.
- Building real things leads you to use open source projects, which leads to hitting problems, which leads to good issues and contributions.
- He says you need to know the thing well enough to judge whether your solution works.

chunks.heading: Goal-setting lesson for new developers
chunks.text:
- Theo says new developers set bad goals like "make an open source contribution" or "learn JavaScript". You don't understand these well enough to know when you've achieved them.
- Goals should come from things you understand, such as a game you play or an app you want to recreate, so you can tell when it's working.
- His rule: "work backwards" from something you understand rather than setting a goal in something you don't.
- He points to his separate goal-setting video for more on this.
- Refusing to learn TypeScript while chasing contributions is, to him, a symptom of this: a developer who won't do the hard thing and treats open source as a hack.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo argues good engineering managers act as buffers who set engineers up for success. The core levers are trust, letting people fail safely, protecting team energy, and making it safe to ask dumb questions during onboarding. He uses Luke Lafreniere at LTT as an example of a non-coder leading tech well.

chunks.heading: Trust as the core job of an engineering manager
chunks.text:
- Theo says almost every management decision he makes is aimed at building trust across the company.
- He makes sure everyone on the team is bought in, understands what's going on, and feels trusted in the work they contribute.
- If anyone has reservations about how something is being built, he wants the team to discuss it openly.
- His stated philosophy: "strong opinions weekly held". It doesn't matter if the person is a principal tech lead from Amazon with eight years there or a brand-new intern. If someone has a strong belief and can back it up, everyone should listen and learn from it.
- He frames the aim of management as smoothing the roughness between engineers and everyone else (CEO, product, design, users) and setting engineers up for success.

chunks.heading: Let engineers fail
chunks.text:
- Theo calls letting engineers fail one of the best things an engineering manager can do, especially when you know they're going to fail.
- There are three outcomes when someone pushes a strong opinion: they're right and the team learns, they're wrong and you teach them, or (the underrated option) they're wrong, they're hard to convince, and you let them go be wrong for a bit.
- If you know a technology an engineer wants to adopt won't work and will fail early, you can say so, but if they don't listen, let them do it.
- Reasons he gives:
  - It shows you trust them.
  - They might be right, and then you get to adopt the better solution.
  - If they're wrong, they build trust and capability, and make better-informed recommendations next time.
- Caveat: if someone consistently pushes bad things and consistently breaks stuff, that's a different conversation.
- He thinks most engineers aren't given enough leash, especially when the manager has a technical background.
- He admits it's been hard to manage teams where the engineers know more and are more tuned in than he is, and says he's consistently surprised by how capable they are.

chunks.heading: Energy is the most valuable resource a team has
chunks.text:
- Theo argues codebases don't live or die on technology choices or on how good the hired engineers are. They live or die on who has the energy to keep things moving through maintenance windows, hard problems and all the pain a project has until it finds its users in the state it needs to be in.
- He says managers too easily throw this away by saying no to an energized engineer because their idea doesn't immediately line up with business goals.
- His claim: "there is no business goal that isn't accelerated by a team that's energized by the work they're doing". Even if the thing bringing the energy points in a different direction, that energy gets you where you want to go much faster.
- He says this is the reason startups can exist at all. Companies like Twitch could in principle "run circles around" a two-person startup, but they can't because people with energy get burnt out before they can apply it.
- The manager's job:
  - Find the people bringing energy.
  - Give them everything they need to maintain it and share it with the team.
  - Manage the team's energy and excitement, and be willing to take big risks and get into fights with executives to protect it.
- He sees devs who learn for fun (e.g. those watching his videos as soon as they drop) as having exactly the energy a company needs, and thinks managers should feed into the people who care enough to keep learning in their free time and bring it back to the team.

chunks.heading: Case study: Luke Lafreniere at Linus Tech Tips / Floatplane
chunks.text:
- Theo holds up Luke as a stellar example of engineering management, noting it doesn't always look like someone who's coded for 10 years.
- Luke recently became CTO of all of LTT, having never been a real engineer, never coded for a living and never had an engineering manager himself. He ended up in charge of building Floatplane.
- Theo's description of how Luke operates:
  - He knows nearly every engineer he hires is better than him, embraces that, and uses it to improve.
  - His main role is translating between developer speak and timelines, communicating to the rest of LTT what the engineers need. Theo notes that on the business side deadlines get hit, while in tech "deadlines are imaginary".
  - He explores new things and brings them to the team. He became a regular viewer of Theo's channel to find things to bring in, and noticed what the team needed.
  - He brought Vercel and Next.js technology to Floatplane and LTT because he thought they'd add value.
- Results Theo cites:
  - Researching and adopting those technologies gave his engineers excitement and motivation to keep iterating.
  - It significantly widened the pool of engineers they could hire, and raised the energy level of people coming in.
- Theo says Luke reached out because he had no other engineering managers to talk to. They had a four-hour Discord call, and most of it was Theo reinforcing what Luke was already doing.
- Theo says Luke's YouTube-grind background taught him how important energy is, and he pushes to maintain it on the team.
- Theo is now excitedly referring engineers to Luke for the next era of LTT.

chunks.heading: The dumb question rule for onboarding
chunks.text:
- Theo enforces a rule with new teammates: they must ask a minimum number of dumb questions every day for their first couple of weeks. His example is at least two dumb questions every work day.
- The reasoning:
  - It feels awful to be stuck on something you feel you should know, like it should be in a doc somewhere or was said before and you missed it.
  - A big part of development is feeling dumb, and it's the manager's job to help people through that.
  - Feeling dumb for too long drains energy, so providing a comfortable way to work through it preserves it.
- The things that typically hold people up are dumb ones, such as getting a dev environment set up or figuring out which GitHub account to sign in with, and most engineers are scared to ask about them.
- Forcing people through those questions makes them far more excited to contribute by the end of their first week.
- He claims he has seen this take month-plus onboarding windows and knock them down to a few days.

chunks.heading: Summary of what makes a team successful
chunks.text:
- Theo's three takeaways: let people fail, build trust, and feed into the people who bring energy.
- He says team value doesn't come from how many tickets close each week or how good the top engineer is at TypeScript. It comes from cohesiveness, focus, trust and the energy people bring.
- He frames it as the manager's job to make people comfortable and excited to bring all of that to the workplace.
- He notes that many engineering managers don't think about engineering management at all, much less in a way that's cohesive and conducive to growth for their engineers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo reacts live to a YouTuber who reverse engineered UploadThing and rebuilt it in a day. He explains the architecture (signed S3 policies, direct client-to-S3 uploads, callbacks) and why the backend callback must be the source of truth. He also shows how he treats copycats and open source: celebrate it, don't hide.

chunks.heading: Why UploadThing's backend-first `onUploadComplete` callback matters
chunks.text:
Theo built UploadThing, a service that makes S3 file uploads easy for developers, and says its backend-first callback is a deliberate design choice.

- He saw a recurring problem at Twitch and "in many code bases": apps use S3 pre-signed POST URLs but don't record the file until the client finishes uploading and tells the server "hey by the way I'm done uploading."
- A client can get the pre-signed URL, block calls back to the service, post to S3 anyway, and the completion message never goes through. The result is ghost files sitting in the bucket that aren't logged in the database.
- UploadThing's `onUploadComplete` callback runs from the backend. He says to use it "as the source of truth in your database." You should never have a file uploaded that you aren't logging somewhere, or you "run the risk of lost files."
- Client-side callbacks (showing the URL in the UI) are fine for display, but he says not to rely on them as the source of truth. A user could also change the URL they post to your endpoint and swap in something you never approved. He "highly, highly" recommends handling this on your backend.

chunks.heading: How the upload flow works and why it skips your infrastructure
chunks.text:
Theo describes the architecture and says a main thing UploadThing optimizes for is not forcing devs to pay egress on file bytes.

1. The client sends only file metadata (file keys, sizes, types) to the dev's own server, not the files.
2. The dev's server validates the metadata against the router rules (file types, max size).
3. The dev's server calls UploadThing's server, which generates a pre-signed POST URL/S3 policy and stores the metadata in a database.
4. The client uploads directly to S3. This is "the important piece because it skips your infrastructure and doesn't cost you any egress."
5. S3 triggers a Lambda bound directly on UploadThing's end, with the uploaded file key. UploadThing translates "the chaos that S3 puts in that metadata" into an actual message.
6. UploadThing looks up the stored metadata and the dev's callback URL, then calls the dev's service back.

- He says you should not have to upload files to your server, because then you "eat the egress" twice: once to send files to your server and again to send them out to S3.
- He credits Mark, who worked at Retool, for knowing how to do the weird S3 bindings.

chunks.heading: Open source, reverse engineering, and being validated by it
chunks.text:
Theo reacts positively to a YouTuber (Josh) reverse engineering UploadThing and building a clone in about 24 hours.

- The source was already readable in the published npm packages. He says he "didn't bother clearing the source out" and "didn't even need to reverse minify," and open sourcing "is more formality than anything."
- The architecture diagram (customer-owned pieces in orange, UploadThing's in blue, Amazon's in orange) is in the repo. He says there was no reason to hide it: "we're not trying to obfuscate everything."
- He feels bad for not publishing the architecture explanation first, since Josh reverse engineered almost the same diagram himself. He had planned to give those resources out.
- He finds it validating that someone cares enough to make resources he didn't. His take: Josh is an S3 expert who "gets the value" and thinks it's cool enough to make a video about, which is the person who matters.
- He promoted Josh's channel ("go subscribe to Josh, he deserves it probably even more than me") and said he'd link the repo, treating it as free distribution and goodwill rather than a threat.

chunks.heading: Owning shipping delays and early-product gaps
chunks.text:
Theo admits missing features the clone had and takes responsibility for the delay.

- Josh's clone had an on-success callback and on-error handling on the client; Theo says UploadThing had added all of this in the most recent release.
- He says it was "a very early demo" and the team hoped to ship more updates the week before, but they were busy at Reactathon and Vercel Ship events and keeping the service running.
- He says "we dropped the ball here much more than I would have liked" and that the component library and API changes "should have happened Wednesday last week... I'll take the L on that for sure."

chunks.heading: Security details of the upload policy
chunks.text:
Theo and Josh's walkthrough covers how the signed policy enforces limits.

- The server generates an S3 policy containing a signature, delivered like a JSON web token; the client cannot change it or the upload "wouldn't work."
- The policy enforces a content-length range (the max bytes the dev configured, e.g. 3 MB) and a content-type prefix such as starting with `image/`.
- Limits must be enforced server side, "because you cannot trust the client to do this."
- After S3 uploads, a notification (like a webhook through Amazon's simple notification service) tells UploadThing the file key and size, which it uses to attribute the upload to an API key and count it against that key's quota. Theo notes UploadThing handles this on the edge with Upstash as the database because it plays well with the edge.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo argues that aspirations like "be an engineer," "learn React," or "contribute to open source" are not goals because they have no clear end. Break them down into concrete deliverables you build, tied to problems you care about, and let the aspirations follow. Passion feeds you through the hard parts, and even failed goals make you a better engineer.

chunks.heading: Why Theo says "be an engineer" and "learn React" are bad goals
chunks.text:
- Theo argues vague aspirations ("become a software engineer", "learn React", "improve test coverage", "contribute to open source") are not goals because they have no clear start or end. Nobody can say when they have "learned React" or "become an engineer".
- He says he is maybe 60-70% through React and is good at it, so "learning" is not a measurable state.
- He treats aspirations as places you end up, not things you drive toward directly.
- He frames engineering goals as specific, pointed deliverables: things you can create and finish.
- He separates intrinsic wants ("I want to be", "I want to learn") from extrinsic goals ("I want to create", "I want to deliver"). Intrinsic ones usually mean "I want to feel like an engineer", which has nowhere to go as a goal.
- His rule: "engineers treat aspirations like goals. Aspirations are not goals." Aspirations are poor drivers; goals with deliverable ends are "a fantastic driver".

chunks.heading: How to turn a vague goal into a deliverable
chunks.text:
Theo's method is to keep asking questions until the goal becomes a thing you can ship.

1. Start with "I want to learn React". Ask what that means: build an app, or get a job? He gives very different advice for each.
2. Pick the app path and ask what app. He tells people to pick a specific thing, not a vague "something".
3. Choose something concrete, such as a Twitter clone, and follow a tutorial for it.
4. Alternatively, build a tool for a problem you personally have. His example: in the game Outriders, a web app where he enters the number of runs and sees how likely a gear piece is to have dropped.
5. You know you have succeeded when the app solves the problem you had.

- His summary: "Building goals around specific problems you can solve will make delivering on them significantly easier."
- Best-practice one-liners he gives: the best way to learn React is to build things with it; the best way to improve test coverage is to write tests around the things that are breaking; the best way to be an engineer is to build things.

chunks.heading: The "circle" model: aspiration on the outside, small goals as points
chunks.text:
- Theo draws a big circle as the aspiration (e.g. "contribute to open source") and a tiny dot in the middle as the new dev.
- A vague goal is a whole ring you are trying to reach, so people wander chaotically. A good goal is a specific point.
- His worked example for open source:
  1. Go through the Deno tutorial.
  2. Build a chat server with Deno.
  3. Hit a bug in the websocket implementation or out-of-date docs.
  4. File a PR to update the docs.
  5. You are now an open source contributor.
- He notes that finding a mistake in the tutorial itself could equally lead to a PR. The aspiration is reached as a side effect of specific goals.
- Those goals are picked because there is something you want to do, not because of the aspiration. Chasing the immediate deliverables is how you reach the higher aspiration.

chunks.heading: Contributing to open source: start from the project, not the goal
chunks.text:
- Theo says "contributing to open source" is "just the straight up wrong way to go about it" as a starting goal.
- Instead, use more packages and try new things. When a doc has a typo, an example is unclear, or you understand a bug and can fix it, that is the moment to contribute.
- Genuine interest in the project first, then contribution, goes much better than choosing to contribute and then hunting for a project.
- He criticises Hacktoberfest for this: it encourages people with no idea what the project is to search by "beginner friendly" tags and throw in contributions hoping something merges. He calls that "the opposite of both good goal setting and meaningful contributions".
- He says the most meaningful contributions come from people who use and care about the thing.

chunks.heading: Detours and failure are still progress
chunks.text:
- Theo's example path: aspire to be an engineer, set a first goal of building a Twitch clone, then find the hard part is the infrastructure (video / WebRTC), not the UI.
- You drift away from learning React but still become a better engineer. He says it is "okay to ignore" the higher-level aspirations in favour of immediate deliverables.
- It is fine to give up on a goal, for example learning enough WebRTC to get video working, then building a calculator instead.
- A better goal wording he suggests: "learn enough WebRTC to have video working", not "learn WebRTC".
- He says how someone handles failure is one of his biggest signals of a successful engineer, more than how many big things they shipped.
- If a candidate fails at every project but discusses it meaningfully in an interview, "I probably hire you still".

chunks.heading: Passion, discipline and the "make money" goal
chunks.text:
- Theo says that if the only goal is money and the person never intends to enjoy the work, his content is not useful to them. He says that is fine and a flaw in him, not them.
- His own claim: he threw away a 400k a year salary to stream on Twitch and run a company, and he loves engineering.
- Engineering "kind of sucks" at times (dev environment fights, React Native not spitting out an app, mobile loading bugs). Being an engineer is a bad goal for that reason: if that is all you are working toward, you will give up.
- Excitement about the thing on the other side makes the pain worth it: "the journey sucks way harder if you don't like the destination", so pick destinations you are excited about and proud of.
- He says do not rely on passion for one specific project. Feed passion generally, and it will carry you through hard parts. If a project kills your passion, a new interest (e.g. WebRTC) can take over.
- Pure discipline can work. His example goal: "get a job at FAANG for greater than 100k a year", driven by studying interviews and Cracking the Coding Interview.
- He warns the risks: you either burn out before getting there, or arrive and have no idea what to do next. He says he has seen many people in that state and has made it a hobby to help them.
- With small goals you keep feeling the highs and lows along the way, instead of one big payoff at the end.

chunks.heading: Examples and why software is different
chunks.text:
- Aiden (a younger dev Theo says is more talented than him): built FossaBot to solve specific problems high-traffic Twitch chats had, then set a goal of keeping hosting costs reasonable, and learned a lot along the way. Theo says his goals are better and his delivery on them is too.
- Jason Docton (Urad project): learned to code to build his charity's website with donation systems and integrations, because paid developers were too expensive and Squarespace was not good enough. The specific goal made him learn and deliver much faster.
- Theo notes even principal engineers ask "how do I learn your stack". His answer: you don't learn it, you build something with it and bring questions.
- Software is unlike law or medicine, where there are direct paths. In software, the indirect path (building things, breaking things, reverse engineering sites) is more effective than the direct one.
- His skateboarding analogy: his goals were "land this trick", "kickflip this stair set", never "be a skateboarder" or "get good at stairs". He brought that mindset to engineering.
- He says developers are closer to musicians and skateboarders than lawyers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo recounts building Mod View at Twitch, a fully customizable moderator dashboard, with two engineers in six months. He explains the inverse portal pattern that preserved widget state across drag and drop, and credits team care for users and a padded deadline for the outcome.

chunks.heading: Mod View: what it was and why it mattered to Theo
chunks.text:
- Mod View is the moderator tool Theo built at Twitch. He calls it his proudest project, ahead of this channel, his work at Ping, or UploadThing.
- It is a fully customizable moderation UI. Moderators move, resize, dock, hide and show widgets such as chat, automod queue, mod actions and predictions.
- Theo describes it as "one of the most successful launches in twitch's history", delivered despite roadblocks that made it "seem like it was doomed for failure".
- It started from internal safety tooling. Theo first built admin panels used to investigate reports and ban users. That internal platform got good enough that the team decided external moderator tools should be as good.
- Theo ranks it above his other work because of both technical innovation and team organization.

chunks.heading: Constraints: shared ownership, short deadline, small team
chunks.text:
- The safety team was close to the chat team, but did not own whispers, channel points, ratings, subscriptions, bits or even the player. Moderators needed all of that data in one place.
- Widgets came from different teams with different opinions on React, including hooks support and external state management.
- Rewriting every team's code to use one shared state manager was possible but not feasible.
- Staffing was Theo plus two additional engineers, with about 6 months to ship.
- Theo had the product manager set the deadline a month early to create a buffer for polish. He says that month "was huge for us" in making the product really good.

chunks.heading: Technical decisions: bet on hooks, fork what is close, compose
chunks.text:
- The team went all in on hooks, functional programming and a composable model. This was late 2018 to early 2019, and they kept that choice as work ramped up through 2019.
- They evaluated what neighboring teams used. The dashboard team used react-mosaic for resizing and moving panes.
- react-mosaic had no concept of open/close or reuse, and it remounted children when things moved, losing their state. It "introduced as many problems as it solved", but its UI capabilities were good enough that they used it.
- Theo internally forked react-mosaic and added what was missing.
- They used react-dnd for the hooks and primitives behind the widget bar, reorderable side nav and dragging elements in and out of Mosaic. Making these interact took deep understanding of both the forked Mosaic code and react-dnd, which they kept up to date.

chunks.heading: The state problem and the inverse portal solution
chunks.text:
- Problem: moving a widget unmounts and remounts it, so components like chat lose state (messages vanish). Teams outside his own owned the widgets, so he could not move their state to a global store.
- Theo's solution: widgets are never mounted where they appear.
  - All possible widgets, including those not currently shown, are mounted once in a hidden, stable list in the virtual DOM.
  - The visible layout renders only an "out portal" (placeholder) for each widget.
  - Moving a widget moves the out portal's location, not the component, so state survives drags, hides and re-renders.
- He frames it as in portals (where you mount) and out portals (where it appears). The React tree keeps one stable parent while the real DOM places the element elsewhere.
- Origin: he proposed it "somewhat chaotically" from using portals for odd things before. He nearly shut it down when it did not seem viable. His manager asked to try it, found Theo's dumb mistakes, and got it working.
- It is still the pattern that keeps Mod View state persistent regardless of UI customization.

chunks.heading: Performance testing at scale
chunks.text:
- Mod View sometimes leaked memory for very large streamers.
- Theo had roughly six laptops and four desktops on his desk, running custom builds against very large streams to find the leaks.
- He says this dedication came from caring about the users: "that level of dedication ... it was so much effort but we did it because we cared so much".

chunks.heading: Why it succeeded, in Theo's words
chunks.text:
- Main reason: "everyone working on it cared". The whole team was aligned that moderators deserve better tools.
- Moderators "make the content that we do possible" and "keep twitch safe". Theo says his own chat would be unmanageable without his moderators.
- Success factors he lists:
  - Patterns that fit the problem (hooks, composition, portals).
  - Libraries forked and built on rather than rewritten.
  - A small team genuinely invested in the users.
  - A deadline with real buffer built in.
- He also notes the project worked because the team did not wait for perfect architecture. They fit the solution to the organization (many teams, no shared state manager) instead of forcing a rewrite.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo's first conference talk gives a framework for picking technology: measure cost (ramp up, maintenance, off-boarding), value, and risk against where the team and business are heading. He compares tRPC, GraphQL, Redwood and create-t3-app to show why modular choices keep the cost of leaving cheap.

chunks.heading: Framework for evaluating technical decisions: cost, value, risk
chunks.text:
Theo argues picking tech is an investment, like hiring an employee: you are betting on the people maintaining it (or on your ability to fork it), and it affects hiring, developer satisfaction, delivery time and what you can build. His position is that more options don't make decisions inherently harder; they just mean you need a better way to measure them. He measures every option on three axes:

- **Cost**, split into three parts:
  - ramp-up time
  - maintenance over time
  - ramp-off (migration) cost
- **Value**: time saved, wins users feel, developer happiness, and effect on hiring.
- **Risk**: kept separate from cost. Theo describes it as "almost like the delta for how much range there is for the cost to be in." It is the hardest to measure, but he says to measure both the risk of a technology and your team's tolerance for it. Decide this loosely ahead of time so you can discuss it and reflect on it.

chunks.heading: Plotting cost against team size to compare technologies
chunks.text:
Theo's visualization puts cost on the vertical axis (time, money and a hint of risk, i.e. how much drain on the people building and how much less time goes to user-facing features). On the horizontal axis he uses employee count.

- Employee count is imperfect, but it is a way to think about how a project will change over time.
- A side project with a friend will never have 100 people on it. A greenfield project at work might go to 50 people in weeks and hundreds later. The technologies should differ.
- Companies that know they need 2,000 employees in a few years choose differently from a small, successful team that chooses a simple codebase by design.
- Risk shows up as horizontal stretching or shrinking of the curve: how soon you have to adopt or drop a technology.

chunks.heading: tRPC: cheap to leave, bounded in scale
chunks.text:
Theo calls tRPC one of the best ways to start a new full stack app. It is a type-safe API defined with plain TypeScript functions, with no custom language and no compiler, which makes sweeping changes fast because inference shows errors on both sides.

- **Ramp-up:** somewhat high. You need to understand it well, and there is boilerplate. Usually one person sets it up and the rest of the team cruises on top.
- **Maintenance:** effectively flat as the team grows. You just write functions and call them.
- **Limit:** with enough endpoints, the TypeScript compiler slows to a crawl and eventually crashes from the amount of inference. There are codebase sizes where tRPC is not valid, so plan early for moving off it.
- **Risk:** it is mostly the work of one developer. Theo accepts that because the migration cost is low: porting to GraphQL or Express means copy-pasting existing functions and adding your own validation and schema.
- **His own call:** at ping (5 people) he optimizes for shipping functions fast and will pay the migration cost later, "when there is a technology that makes more sense for us as the team and the codebase grows."
- **Requirement:** it only works well if backend and frontend are both TypeScript.

chunks.heading: GraphQL: expensive to adopt, huge to leave, valuable as team communication
chunks.text:
- **Ramp-up:** much higher, because you are choosing "like five" technologies (client, server, and so on). Prescriptive options like Apollo "tend to fail faster." Theo says he could draw 15 lines on the chart for different GraphQL setups.
- **Maintenance:** every schema change carries a cost, because clients may be in other codebases and you never have a firm guarantee they will respect the change. He watched Twitch pay this regularly.
- **Value:** at Twitch it was worth it. Its benefit was "a method for us to communicate better and define standards between the backend and front-end teams," not a technology that magically solves problems.
- **Risk reduction:** the schema language came from Meta and has a huge community, with clients and servers for Swift, Kotlin, Python, Go, and so on.
- **Ramp-off:** "if we ever had to move off of GraphQL we're screwed." Once deeply bought in, he finds it unimaginable to move off.

chunks.heading: RedwoodJS vs create-t3-app: how far each scales and what leaving costs
chunks.text:
- **RedwoodJS:** a full stack TypeScript framework with a strong GraphQL layer. Theo thinks it scales to larger teams than tRPC or create-t3-app because of that layer.
  - Non-TypeScript hires or Swift and Kotlin mobile clients can consume the same APIs.
  - Most of the GraphQL definition and consumption lives inside the Redwood project, so when you hit its cap, moving off is very expensive.
- **create-t3-app:** a project his community built, on his idea, to cut tRPC onboarding cost. It bootstraps the boilerplate and the interactions between pieces like NextAuth and Prisma, so that knowledge is "paid off in advance" by the maintainers.
  - Maintenance cost is the same, since the technology is the same.
  - Off-boarding is slightly more expensive, because you need to understand tRPC better at that point.
  - Setup asks which pieces you want (tRPC, Prisma, Tailwind, NextAuth), and you can add, remove or swap them later.
- **Comparison on his chart:** over the life of a growing company, create-t3-app costs less time, effort and sanity than tRPC alone. Redwood reaches a similar cost at the point where create-t3-app is outgrown. At around 400 employees (he stresses this is arbitrary), the cost of leaving Redwood is far higher. Once you have paid to move off create-t3-app, you are roughly where Redwood sits.
- **Theo's summary:** he says modular tools are cheap to move off, "you can move to anything else at that point," and that composability is "the easiest way to reduce the risk of any technology bet that you make."

chunks.heading: Other factors beyond the cost curve: clients, team, future
chunks.text:
- **Client needs:** users are the often-forgotten part. Engineers talk about raw numbers like latency, but he says to think about what users need now and later. His example is the Amazon figure where a couple hundred milliseconds cost roughly 10% of checkouts.
- **Current team:** consider what they know and how the choice affects their day-to-day satisfaction. Even as an opinionated leader, he would let an engineer adopt a technology they are confident in and he is unsure of, even if it might burn and fail. Developer satisfaction is "essential to retaining your team."
- **Future:** know where the project is expected to be.
  - Many of his projects are solo.
  - Some may have all his code deleted and replaced by the 10,000th engineer.
  - Modularity and tech picks should match that expected trajectory.
- **Examples of risk that extends reach:** hiring non-engineers, or having contractors on iOS and Android who need the data, can favor something like Redwood. A huge endpoint count even with a small team can force an earlier move off tRPC.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Theo joins Peter Steinberger at an OpenClaw meetup Q&A. He argues running a company with payroll and investors removes freedom, while open source keeps you free to say no and experiment. He also pushes users to donate to the projects they rely on and founders to launch every small ship loudly.

chunks.heading: Commercialization and keeping OpenClaw free and open source
chunks.text:
The speaker in this source is Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator); Theo's contributions are the founder and open-source commentary below. Theo says that running your own company is a common misconception of freedom:

- "People seem to think like when you run your own company, you get more freedom somehow. But it's actually the exact opposite."
- A company means a payroll to meet, employees who need enough (but not too much) work, benefits to handle, and income to guarantee pay.
- It also means investors who need to see growth that gives them a chance of making money back.
- "I have never felt more like my day was like locked in and controlled by external forces as I have as a founder running a company."

chunks.heading: Why open source is freer than a company
chunks.text:
Theo argues open source is "way more freeing even if you have users that are upset with you."

- It is easier to say no when you have users than when you have investors.
- Open source is "the safest way to figure this out."
- Companies have to take certain paths because of external pressures, and the opportunity to experiment shrinks when that happens.
- He frames staying open as protecting the ability to experiment.

chunks.heading: Fund the open source you actually use
chunks.text:
Theo calls out the gap between what people spend and what they give the projects they rely on:

- He asked the room to raise a hand if they bought a Mac Mini for OpenClaw; many did (about $700 each).
- Then he asked who donated to the project; "a much smaller number."
- His line: "You can spend $700 on a Mac you didn't need. You can't spend $5 a month on the project."
- People spend about $200 a month across three AI subscriptions but pay nothing for the project that brought them there.
- He asks people to donate to the open source projects they depend on.

chunks.heading: Launch more, and launch every surface
chunks.text:
Theo advises Peter to be louder about shipping:

- "You got to launch more." The market is at a point where companies announce a dark mode for one page.
- Each surface (iOS app, iPadOS app, Android app) has different users and deserves its own launch.
- Each launch should be watched daily, with a short video posted on Twitter.

chunks.heading: Self-adapting software and the AI labs
chunks.text:
Theo's views on where agentic software is heading:

- He likes the idea of agents making changes on your machine from plain language; setting up a new Linux machine was more fun with tools that modify it for you.
- He notes the big labs want to let agents run with more trust (he cites Sam Altman moving from checking every command to running Codex in yolo mode and leaving it on), but they can't be the ones to say so.
- That makes it valuable to see someone push the opposite extreme and show how far these things can go.
- He thinks one of Peter's advantages is being slightly outside the AI hype: coming in later, he wasn't distracted by MCPs and fine-tuning, and could mix some AI with "a little bit of the crazy" that the big labs wouldn't dare ship.
